A.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
A.q: Which five features define a benign tumour?
opts: Autonomous growth, clonal origin, parenchyma and stroma, a single genetic alteration, no stimulus needed
Those are the features of a neoplasm generally, benign or malignant.
Pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses, abnormal differentiation, and invasion
Those are the histological features that move a tumour towards malignancy.
Circumscribed, compresses, often encapsulated, well differentiated, no metastasis, slow
Correct — each has a malignant counterpart on the same slide: ragged border, infiltrates and invades, various degrees of differentiation, may metastasize, grows rapidly.
Ragged border, infiltrates surrounding tissue, no capsule, variably differentiated, may metastasize, grows rapidly
That is the malignant list, which is the contrast being drawn.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Which tinea subtype affects the nails, and what is its other name?
opts: Tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis
Correct. Corporis is trunk and limbs, pedis foot, cruris groin, capitis head, facialis face, manuum hand, barbae beard.
Tinea capitis, also called onychomycosis
Tinea capitis affects the head.
Tinea manuum, affecting the nails of the hand
Tinea manuum affects the hand rather than the nails specifically.
Tinea barbae, affecting nails and beard
Tinea barbae affects the beard area.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: How do gentamicin and tobramycin damage hearing, and which frequencies go first?
opts: They cross-link DNA in the stria vascularis, disturbing endolymph ion homeostasis
That is the platinum chemotherapy mechanism — cisplatin and carboplatin.
Reactive oxygen species destroy outer hair cells from the base, so high pitches go first
Correct. The base of the cochlea encodes high frequencies, so basal damage shows as high-frequency loss. The mechanism is oxidative injury, not a direct toxic binding.
They alter the stria vascularis potential reversibly
That is the loop diuretic effect, and reversibility is what separates it from the aminoglycosides.
They inhibit the prestin motor protein in outer hair cells
Inhibiting prestin in outer hair cells is the salicylate mechanism, and its hallmark is tinnitus rather than permanent threshold loss.

A.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
A.q: What is the hallmark of dry, atrophic macular degeneration?
opts: Cotton-wool spots in the nerve fibre layer
Those are an ischaemic finding in retinopathy.
Drusen — discrete yellow extracellular debris beneath the pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane
Correct — with its composition and location.
Choroidal neovascularisation breaching upward into the subretinal space
That is the wet form.
Neovascularisation on the optic disc
That is proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

A.io: h — Describe the steps of chemical carcinogenesis
A.q: Which carcinogens are produced by the combustion of tobacco, and what do they cause?
opts: Aromatic amines, causing bladder and lung cancer; among the most powerful carcinogens known
Aromatic amines are classically emphasised in OCCUPATIONAL bladder cancer.
Nitrosamines, causing gastric and oesophageal cancer
Nitrosamines are not the agents produced by tobacco combustion.
Aflatoxins, causing hepatocellular carcinoma
Aflatoxin is not among the chemical carcinogens listed here.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, causing bladder and lung cancer
Correct — among the most powerful carcinogens known, and tobacco smoke contains numerous others besides.

A.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
A.q: What does the abbreviation PMN refer to?
opts: All granulocytes
Correct. Polymorphonuclear leukocyte, abbreviated PMN, is used to refer to all granulocytes rather than to neutrophils alone.
Neutrophils only
Neutrophils are the most numerous granulocyte, but the term covers all of them.
All mononuclear leucocytes
Mononuclear leucocyte is the alternative name for the agranulocytes, the opposite grouping.
Plasma cells and memory B cells
Neither is a granulocyte.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Fibrinous inflammation forms a thick meshwork that can be removed only by what, and what happens if that removal fails?
opts: Complement fragment C3b; failure results in ulceration
C3b is an opsonin, and ulceration is a separate pattern involving necrosis and sloughing of surface epithelium.
Macrophage digestion; failure results in gangrene
Gangrenous inflammation is a severe form of necrosis, not a consequence of retained fibrin.
Phagocytosis by neutrophils; failure produces pus
Pus is the defining content of the suppurative pattern, not a consequence of failed fibrinolysis.
Fibrolytic enzymes; failure results in scar tissue formation
Correct. The meshwork can only be removed by fibrolytic enzymes, and failure of this results in scar tissue formation.

A.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
A.q: What happens in familial adenomatosis polyposis syndrome, and by what age does cancer develop?
opts: Hundreds to thousands of premalignant polyps young, then colon cancer by fifty
Correct — five hundred to two thousand five hundred adenomatous polyps in the teens and twenties. The responsible gene is adenomatous polyposis coli.
Patients develop a single premalignant polyp in childhood, and colon cancer by age thirty
The polyp burden described is in the hundreds to thousands.
Patients develop multiple neurofibromas at puberty, and sarcoma by age forty
That describes the neurofibromatosis picture instead.
Patients develop skin cancer in sun-exposed areas from early childhood
That is xeroderma pigmentosum.

A.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
A.q: What is a biomaterial in this context?
opts: Anything not human that is put into a human
Correct. That is the working definition given, and it is why the opsonisation point generalises across implanted devices.
Any material that has been sterilised before implantation
Sterility is a separate property; the example turns on the response occurring despite it.
Any tissue harvested from the patient's own body
Autologous tissue is not what the parenthetical describes.
Any protein produced during the inflammatory response
Mediators and opsonins are proteins of the response, not biomaterials.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: What can a myopic patient see well?
opts: Objects up close
Correct — myopia is nearsightedness, so near vision is the preserved one.
Objects far away
Distance vision is the impaired one in myopia.
Neither near nor far without correction
Near vision is preserved.
Only objects at the extreme periphery
Myopia is a refractive, not a field, problem.

A.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
A.q: A temporal lobe lesion affecting part of the optic radiation produces which defect?
opts: Contralateral inferior quadrantanopsia instead
The temporal radiation carries the superior field.
Bitemporal hemianopsia
That is a chiasmal lesion.
Monocular blindness
That requires a prechiasmal lesion.
Contralateral superior quadrantanopsia, or pie in the sky
Correct — site D, in the temporal loop of the optic radiation.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: What are the two phases of allergic contact dermatitis?
opts: Irritation, then hyperkeratosis of the stratum corneum
That describes irritant contact dermatitis and lichenification respectively.
Radial growth, then vertical growth
Those are the growth phases of melanoma.

Sensitization, in which Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells to create specialised memory; and elicitation, in which re-exposure to the same hapten promotes T cell migration and cutaneous inflammation
Correct — a delayed hypersensitivity reaction occurring 48 to 72 hours after exposure. Nickel and poison ivy are the examples.
Sensitization by mast cell degranulation, followed by elicitation through the release of histamine into the surrounding dermal tissue on every subsequent exposure to that same allergen thereafter
That is the immunoglobulin E pathway of urticaria, not the T cell pathway here.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: What is the sequence by which Eustachian tube dysfunction creates negative middle ear pressure?
opts: The tympanic membrane becomes stiff and pulls the ossicles inward
Retraction is a consequence of the negative pressure, not its cause.
The tube fails to open, so the mucosa absorbs the gases
Correct. The middle ear is an air-filled space; if it is not re-ventilated, the mucosa absorbs the gases and the pressure falls. That negative pressure is the start of the otitis media sequence.
Mucus production increases faster than the tube can drain it
Fluid accumulates later, but the initiating step described is gas absorption after failure to ventilate.
Bacterial infection erodes the tube lining and opens it permanently
A patulous tube is a different problem; here the failure is that it does not open.

A.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
A.q: Which set of causes belongs to sensorineural rather than conductive loss?
opts: Eustachian tube dysfunction, middle ear effusion and stapes fixation
All three are conductive: effusion loads the drum with mass, and stapes fixation stiffens the chain. None involves the cochlea or the nerve.
Presbycusis, ototoxic drugs, noise trauma and acoustic neuroma
Correct. All four damage the cochlea or the nerve. Note acoustic neuroma sits here because cranial nerve VIII is part of the sensorineural pathway even though the tumour is outside the cochlea.
Cerumen impaction, otosclerosis, otitis media and tympanic membrane perforation
All four are conductive — they obstruct, load, stiffen or interrupt the sound-conducting apparatus.
Cholesteatoma, exostoses, foreign body and ossicular necrosis
Again all conductive, and they map onto the four core mechanisms of conductive loss.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Which protein deficiency contributes to atopic dermatitis, and what does it reflect?
opts: Insufficient elastin, reflecting loss of recoil
Elastin degradation is part of atrophy.
Insufficient keratohyalin, reflecting loss of the granular layer
Loss of the stratum granulosum is described for psoriasis.
Insufficient filaggrin, reflecting a compromised epidermal barrier
Correct, alongside an overactive immune system and genetic, environmental and psychogenic factors.
Insufficient collagen, reflecting fibroblast failure
Collagen loss relates to atrophy and ulceration rather than eczema.

A.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
A.q: Which dermal cell mediates immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation?
opts: The fibroblast
Fibroblasts produce collagen.
The melanocyte
Melanocytes produce pigment and sit in the epidermis.
The keratinocyte
Keratinocytes form the bulk of the epidermis and produce keratin.
The mast cell
Correct, and its degranulation is the mechanism behind both the wheal and urticaria.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Trauma versus a bee sting illustrates which distinction within acute inflammation?
opts: Inflammation that resolves completely versus inflammation that becomes chronic
Chronicity is determined by persistent infection, toxic agents or autoimmunity rather than by this contrast.
Serous versus fibrinous exudate
The exudate patterns are a separate axis and are not what this pairing illustrates.
Endogenous versus exogenous toxic agents
That contrast is drawn with atherosclerosis and silica, under chronic inflammation.
Damage that is purely physical versus damage that involves activation of an immune response
Correct. Both produce acute inflammation, but only one recruits an immune response, which is the point of the pairing.

A.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
A.q: Which mediator is distinguished from histamine and serotonin by also producing pain?
opts: Immunoglobulin G
Immunoglobulin G is the antibody opsonin recognised through Fc receptors.
Fibrinogen
Fibrinogen forms the meshwork of the fibrinous pattern.
Bradykinin
Correct. All three raise permeability, but pain is listed only for bradykinin — along with a possible increase in leukocyte chemotaxis.
Complement component C3b
C3b acts as an opsonin, binding foreign material for recognition.

A.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
A.q: What defines a secondary skin lesion?
opts: Any lesion that is palpable rather than flat
Palpability separates macules from papules within the primary group.
Any lesion that arises from malignant rather than from benign underlying disease processes
Neither category implies anything about malignancy.
A modification or change of a primary lesion caused by infection, trauma or other factors
Correct, which is why a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble what it came from.
Any lesion appearing on a second body site after the first
Location has nothing to do with the classification.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
A.q: Is metastatic spread random?
opts: No — but only because lymphatic drainage is anatomically fixed
Lymphatic anatomy is one factor, but the point is about spread in general.
No — it is determined by blood flow, receptors, and genetically determined fitness
Correct — this is the headline.
Yes — circulating cells lodge in whichever capillary bed they reach first
This is explicitly wrong.
Yes for haematogenous spread, no for lymphatic spread
The statement is not split that way.

A.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
A.q: What do B lymphocytes do?
opts: Cell-mediated killing of virus-infected cells through T cell receptors
That is the role of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells.
Returning immune function to its normal operation after infection, and preventing autoimmunity
That is the regulatory (suppressor) T cell.
Releasing histamine to increase vascular permeability
Histamine release is attributed to basophils among the leukocytes.
Making antibodies against antigens, acting as antigen-presenting cells, and developing into memory B cells
Correct. All three are listed, and the B lymphocyte is described as playing a large role in the humoral immune response and being essential to adaptive immunity.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: Which two ototoxic effects are described as reversible or symptom-limited rather than permanent?
opts: Noise trauma and presbycusis
Both are irreversible — noise causes stereocilia degeneration and hair cell apoptosis.
Furosemide on the strial potential; salicylate on prestin
Correct. The loop diuretic effect on the strial potential is reversible, and the salicylate effect on the outer hair cell motor protein produces tinnitus. Neither destroys the cells outright.
Gentamicin and tobramycin damage
Aminoglycoside destruction of outer hair cells is the permanent one.
Cisplatin and carboplatin damage
Platinum agents cause bilateral permanent sensorineural loss.

A.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
A.q: Which inherited defect underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, and what is the consequence?
opts: Defective apoptosis genes, so damaged cells cannot self destruct; increased risk of lymphoma
Apoptosis genes are a category, but this is not the disease attached to them here.
Defective protooncogenes, so growth signalling is lost; increased risk of aplasia
Loss of protooncogene function would not produce cancer this way.
Defective repair genes, so ultraviolet B damage cannot be repaired
Correct — the consequence is an increased risk of skin cancer in sun-exposed areas. It is a repair-gene disease rather than a tumour suppressor one.
Defective tumour suppressor genes, so cell growth cannot be inhibited; increased risk of nervous system tumours
That describes the neurofibromatosis genes.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 40

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: In the organ of Corti, what physically opens the tip-link channels on the hair cells?
opts: Shearing of the stereocilia against the tectorial membrane

Correct. Basilar membrane displacement bends the stereocilia against the rigid tectorial membrane, and that mechanical deflection is what opens the channels. Everything upstream exists to produce that shear.
Stapes vibration transmitted directly to the hair cells
The stapes vibrates the oval window, which starts pressure waves in the scala vestibuli. Several steps separate that from the cilia.
Direct pressure of endolymph on the hair cell body
Endolymph displacement moves the membrane, but the channel opens because the cilia are bent against a rigid structure, not from fluid pressure on the cell.
Glutamate binding to the hair cell
Glutamate is released BY the hair cell onto cranial nerve VIII fibres after depolarisation. It is the output, not the trigger.

A.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
A.q: Eosinophils primarily deal with which category of infection, and predominate in which reactions?
opts: Bacterial infection; predominating in suppurative inflammation
Bacterial defence and pus formation are neutrophil functions.
Parasitic infection; predominating in allergic reactions such as asthma, hay fever and hives
Correct. Parasitic infection, with predominance in allergic reactions.
Viral infection; predominating in cell-mediated immunity
Virus-infected cells are handled by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells.
Fungal infection; predominating in chronic granulomatous inflammatory processes
Neutrophils are described as defending against fungal as well as bacterial infection.

A.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
A.q: Which three structures make up the uvea?
opts: The choroid, the retina and the sclera
The retina is the inner tunic and the sclera the outer.
The ciliary body, the lens and the zonules
The lens and zonules are not part of the uvea.
The iris, the cornea and the conjunctiva
The cornea is fibrous and the conjunctiva is a mucosal covering.
The choroid, the ciliary body and the iris
Correct — the vascular middle tunic in full.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Eczematous dermatitis results from which type of inflammatory reaction?
opts: Neutrophil-driven suppurative inflammation
That would produce pustules.
Complement-mediated vessel destruction
That describes a vasculitis.
T cell-mediated
Correct — a chronic condition with frequent or infrequent flares, known as the itch that rashes.
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation alone
That is the urticaria mechanism.

A.io: f — Compare and contrast the different types of malignant tumors according to origin
A.q: What do the prefixes leio- and rhabdo- mean in a sarcoma's name?
opts: Leio- is bone; rhabdo- is cartilage
Neither prefix refers to bone or cartilage.
Leio- is glandular; rhabdo- is squamous
Adeno- is the glandular prefix, and squamous has no such prefix.
Leio- is smooth muscle; rhabdo- is skeletal muscle
Correct — and adeno- means glandular, while the suffix -oma simply means tumour.
Leio- is skeletal muscle; rhabdo- is smooth muscle
The two prefixes are reversed here.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: What are the two pathophysiological causes of strabismus?
opts: Lens opacification and loss of the red reflex
That is cataract.
Extraocular muscle imbalance and cranial nerve palsy of the third, fourth or sixth nerves
Correct — those two mechanisms.
Retinal detachment and vitreous haemorrhage
Neither causes misalignment.
Raised intraocular pressure with progressive optic disc cupping and field loss
That is glaucoma.

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: What is amblyopia?
opts: Ocular misalignment arising from extraocular muscle imbalance or nerve palsy
That is strabismus, which is the contrast to amblyopia.
Progressive optic neuropathy from raised pressure
That is glaucoma.
Opacification of the crystalline lens
That is cataract.
Reduced best-corrected visual acuity from abnormal visual processing during the critical developmental period
Correct — it is a visual deficit rather than a mechanical one.

A.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
A.q: What drives the change from non-proliferative to proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
opts: Rising intraocular pressure forces new vessels to form
Pressure is not the driver.
Accumulation of lipofuscin and apolipoprotein beneath the pigment epithelium
That is drusen formation in macular degeneration.
Bacterial collagenase digestion of the retinal surface
That mechanism belongs to corneal ulceration.
Severe ischaemia upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor, producing neovascularisation
Correct — ischaemia to growth factor to new vessels.

A.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
A.q: What is cancer, and where does the word come from?
opts: A neoplasm that has metastasized; from the Greek for wandering, because cells migrate
Metastasis is a feature many cancers develop, not the definition of the word.
A precancerous lesion; from the Latin for disorder, because architecture is lost
Loss of architecture describes dysplasia, which is not cancer.
A malignant neoplasm; from the Latin for crab
Correct — so named because it adheres to any tissue it seizes upon and reaches out with claws, invading surrounding tissue.
Any neoplasm at all; from the Latin for growth, because the mass enlarges without a stimulus
Cancer is specifically the malignant subset, and the derivation is the crab.

A.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
A.q: Where do impulses travel after leaving the optic nerve?
opts: To the temporal cortex
The temporal lobe carries part of the optic radiation but is not the destination.
To the frontal eye fields
Those govern gaze rather than receiving the visual image.
To the superior colliculus alone
The destination is the visual cortex.
To the occipital cortex
Correct — neural transmission runs to the occipital cortex.

A.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
A.q: What drives dizziness or lightheadedness, as distinct from vertigo?
opts: Cerebral hypoperfusion or metabolic imbalance
Correct. None of these is vestibular, which is why the sensation is of impending faint rather than of the room moving. Getting this distinction right is the first branch point in the whole workup.
Asymmetrical input between the two vestibular apparatus
Asymmetrical vestibular input is the mechanism of vertigo itself, which is the thing dizziness has to be distinguished FROM.
Dislodged otoconia in the semicircular canals
That is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, a vestibular cause.
Endolymphatic hydrops
Endolymphatic hydrops is Meniere disease, which is vestibular — so it produces vertigo rather than the presyncopal sensation of dizziness.

A.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
A.q: Why are there three semicircular canals rather than one?
opts: Each detects a different speed of rotation
The three canals are distinguished by the plane they occupy, not by the speed of rotation they detect.
Two detect rotation and one detects gravity
Gravity and linear acceleration are the otolith organs' job.
Redundancy in case one is damaged
Redundancy is not the explanation. Three canals exist because rotation happens in three planes.
They sit in three planes, so rotation in any direction is detected
Correct. Sagittal, coronal and transverse between them cover all rotational movement.

A.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
A.q: What is the fornix, and why does it matter mechanically?
opts: The dense fibrous plate giving the eyelid its shape
That is the tarsus.
The sphincteric muscle responsible for blinking
That is orbicularis oculi.
The circular junction where the conjunctiva meets the edge of the cornea
That is the limbus.
A flexible junctional cul-de-sac that permits free rotation of the globe
Correct — that is its definition and its mechanical purpose.

A.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
A.q: What is a papilloma?
opts: A tumour with finger-like or warty projections from an epithelial surface
Correct — the projections are visible microscopically or macroscopically.
A tumour forming a glandular pattern or arising from a gland
That is an adenoma.
A malignant tumour arising from supportive, mesenchymal tissue
That is a sarcoma.
A malignant epithelial tumour showing squamous cell differentiation
That is a squamous cell carcinoma.

A.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
A.q: Which sequence correctly orders the cellular events of acute inflammation after stasis?
opts: Transmigration, adhesion, aggregation, phagocytosis, chemotaxis
Adhesion must precede transmigration, and chemotaxis cannot be last.
Aggregation, chemotaxis, transmigration, adhesion, phagocytosis
This inverts nearly the whole sequence.
Leukocyte adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis, aggregation, phagocytosis
Correct. Adhesion to the endothelium precedes movement across it, then directed migration, gathering at the site, and finally ingestion.
Chemotaxis, phagocytosis, adhesion, transmigration, aggregation
Chemotaxis cannot precede the adhesion and transmigration that place the leukocyte in the tissue.

A.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
A.q: What are mesenchymal tumours derived from, and what tissues does that include?
opts: Neural tissue: peripheral nerves, nerve sheaths and the central nervous system
Neural origin is not what mesenchymal means in this classification.
Supportive tissue: connective tissue, adipose tissue, cartilage, smooth and striated muscle, and bone
Correct — the same origin gives sarcomas when the tumour is malignant.
Epithelial surfaces: skin, gastrointestinal lining, respiratory lining and glandular ducts
That is epithelial origin, which gives adenomas and papillomas when benign.
Haematopoietic tissue: bone marrow, lymph nodes, spleen and thymus
Haematopoietic tumours are not the category described here.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 16

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Which histological findings go with chronic inflammation?
opts: White blood cells (lymphocytes and macrophages), proliferation of blood vessels, fibrosis and tissue necrosis
Correct. All four are listed together as the histological associations of chronic inflammation.
Neutrophil predominance with an absence of vascular proliferation
Neutrophils are the leukocyte of acute inflammation; chronic inflammation is accompanied by proliferation of blood vessels.
Eosinophil infiltration with mucus hypersecretion
Eosinophils dominate allergic reactions, and mucus hypersecretion describes the catarrhal pattern.
Serous exudate with low protein content, no cellular infiltrate, and no proliferation of blood vessels
That describes the serous pattern, which occurs early or with mild inflammation.

A.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
A.q: What is the demographic and inheritance pattern of otosclerosis?
opts: Young-to-middle-aged females, accelerated by pregnancy; 50% autosomal dominant
Correct. The pregnancy acceleration is the memorable part, and variable penetrance explains why the family history is often incomplete.
Commonest in young females but entirely sporadic
The demographic is right, but it is not sporadic — 50 per cent is autosomal dominant, with variable penetrance hiding the family history.
Commonest in older males, with no hereditary component
Both halves are wrong: the peak is younger and female, and half of cases are autosomal dominant.
Commonest in children, autosomal recessive
Neither half matches: otosclerosis peaks in young to middle-aged women, and half of cases are autosomal dominant rather than recessive.

A.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
A.q: Which nodal findings require immediate assessment to exclude lymphoma?
opts: Persistent rubbery or matted nodes in older adults
Correct. Reactive nodes are usually tender and follow a regional infection. Rubbery, matted, persistent and supraclavicular in an older patient is the combination that changes the level of concern.
Any palpable cervical node at all
Palpable nodes are common and usually reactive; the features listed are what raise concern.
Tender mobile nodes during a viral upper respiratory infection
That is the ordinary reactive picture, which is usually benign.
Bilateral small nodes in a child with otitis media
Regional response to a head and neck infection — the benign pathway described.

A.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
A.q: Which genes are named as promoting repair of damaged deoxyribonucleic acid?
opts: BRCA-1 and BRCA-2
Correct — a minority of breast cancer patients carry an inherited mutation in one of them.
NF-1 and NF-2
Those are tumour suppressor genes.
Retinoblastoma and adenomatous polyposis coli
Those are also tumour suppressor genes.
p16 and p53
p16 is named under heredity as a tumour suppressor; p53 works in apoptosis.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 30

A.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
A.q: Which glands are involved in an external as opposed to an internal hordeolum?
opts: Both involve the tarsal plate itself rather than any gland
The tarsal plate holds the meibomian glands but is not itself the site.
External involves the glands of Zeis or Moll; internal involves a meibomian gland
Correct — gland by gland, that is the distinction.
External involves a meibomian gland; internal involves the glands of Zeis or Moll
This reverses the assignment.
Both involve the lacrimal gland
The lacrimal gland is not involved in hordeolum.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: In chronic inflammation, what roles do lymphocytes and plasma cells versus macrophages play?
opts: Both populations act solely to proliferate blood vessels
Vascular proliferation accompanies chronic inflammation but is not the function attributed to either cell type.
Lymphocytes and plasma cells mediate antibody production; macrophages process and deliver antigen to immunocompetent cells
Correct. Antibody production belongs to lymphocytes and plasma cells, antigen processing and delivery to macrophages.
Lymphocytes release histamine; macrophages release serotonin
Histamine is attributed to basophils, and neither mediator is assigned to these cells here.
Lymphocytes phagocytose the cellular debris at the site, while macrophages produce and secrete the antibody
This reverses both roles — antibody production is the lymphocyte and plasma cell contribution.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: A patient reacts to a nickel earring 48 to 72 hours after wearing it. Which mechanism does the delay reflect?
opts: An immediate immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation occurring upon the very first contact with the metal
That reaction occurs within minutes and produces wheals.
Direct chemical injury requiring no prior exposure
That is irritant contact dermatitis, which does not require sensitization.
Viral proliferation within basal keratinocytes
That is verrucae vulgaris.
Delayed hypersensitivity requiring T cell migration after re-exposure to a hapten previously presented by Langerhans cells
Correct. The delay is the time the cellular response takes, which is what distinguishes it from an immediate mast cell reaction.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: What is the suspected mechanism of koilonychia?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue producing an opaque nail
That is Terry's nails.
Incomplete keratinization producing white spots
That is leukonychia.
Impaired keratin synthesis associated with deficiency anaemia, weakening the nail plate into raised ridges that are thin and concave
Correct, and the exact pathophysiology is unknown.
A halt of keratin production producing horizontal transverse grooves across the surface of the nail plate itself
That is Beau's lines.

A.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
A.q: What does anaplasia mean?
opts: Disordered growth of epithelium with retained architecture
That is closer to dysplasia, and dysplasia does lose architectural orientation.
Lack of differentiation
Correct — the extreme of the grading scale, with no resemblance to the normal cell.
Close resemblance to the comparable normal cell
That is well differentiated, the opposite end of the scale.
Failure of a primordial tissue to develop into a mature organ
That is aplasia, which is a non-neoplastic developmental abnormality.
A.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 12

A.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
A.q: What can astigmatism combine with, and what happens when it does?
opts: Only presbyopia, and only after the age of forty
Astigmatism is not restricted to combining with presbyopia.
Only glaucoma, through a sustained rise in intraocular pressure over years
There is no such relationship.
Nothing — it always occurs in isolation
It does combine with the other refractive errors.
Myopia or hyperopia, adding a focal-length error to the axis error
Correct — Webster described the two problems stacking.

A.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
A.q: Which cancers is Epstein Barr virus associated with, and which cells does it infect?
opts: B cell lymphomas and nasopharyngeal carcinoma; it infects B lymphocytes
Correct — it immortalizes them, which is the key step, and it also infects epithelial cells of the oropharynx.
Hepatocellular carcinoma; it infects hepatocytes and causes chronic injury with regeneration
That is hepatitis B and hepatitis C.
Cervical carcinoma; it infects cervical epithelium and integrates its genome
That is human papillomavirus.
Gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma; it colonizes the stomach
That is Helicobacter pylori.

A.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
A.q: What is the primary aetiology of TRACTIONAL retinal detachment?
opts: Choroidal melanoma
That is an exudative cause.
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Correct — the neovascular membranes of proliferative disease are the classic traction source.
Severe malignant hypertension
That appears under exudative detachment.
Posterior vitreous detachment
That is a rhegmatogenous risk factor.

A.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
A.q: What does an epidermal inclusion cyst arise from and contain?
opts: A sebaceous gland, and it contains only squalene
The stated origin is the hair follicle and the content is keratin.
A blood vessel, and it contains clotted blood
No such origin is described for this lesion.
A hair follicle, and it contains keratin
Correct. A cyst is an elevated, circumscribed, encapsulated lesion in the dermis or subcutaneous layer with liquid or semisolid contents.
A sweat gland, and it contains sodium and chloride
Eccrine sweat contains those, but the cyst described arises from a follicle.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: How do vocal cord polyps differ from nodules in site and pathogenesis?
opts: Unilateral fibrous calluses from chronic yelling
This mixes the two lesions. Calluses from chronic trauma are nodules and they are bilateral; polyps are unilateral and follow a single event.
Bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma
Bilateral fibrous calluses from chronic phonotrauma are NODULES. Polyps differ on every count — unilateral, soft, and from one event.
Bilateral soft lesions at the anterior commissure from reflux
Neither matches: polyps are unilateral on the middle third and follow acute strain, not bilateral at the commissure from reflux.
Unilateral, soft and pedunculated on the middle third, after one severe strain
Correct. One event rather than chronic repetition, and the healing response is inflammatory rather than a callus. Site and laterality both differ from nodules.

A.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
A.q: Why can an implanted medical device provoke an inflammatory response even when it is sterile?
opts: Because implantation always causes bacterial contamination of surrounding tissue
The point of the example is precisely that the response occurs even when sterile.
Because sterilisation leaves residual endotoxin behind, and that endotoxin then acts as a chemotactic agent
No such residual endotoxin mechanism applies.
Because the material becomes coated with immunoglobulin G and C3b, and immune cells recognise that coating and attach to it
Correct. Opsonisation of the biomaterial is what makes it a target regardless of sterility.
Because the device physically obstructs lymphatic drainage
Lymphatic obstruction is not offered as the mechanism.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: Which cells drive psoriasis, and which cytokines are involved?
opts: Melanocytes proliferate at the dermal-epidermal junction
That is the origin of melanoma.
Active T cells infiltrating the epidermis stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and excessive cytokine production, particularly tumour necrosis factor alpha, interferon gamma and interleukin-12
Correct. It is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory dermatosis, and skin cells multiply up to ten times faster than normal.
Mast cells release histamine which drives keratinocyte proliferation
That is the urticaria pathway and does not produce psoriasis.
Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells, producing a delayed hypersensitivity reaction 48 to 72 hours after each exposure to the allergen in question every single time
That is allergic contact dermatitis.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: Which cytokines drive nasal polyp formation, and which cell floods the tissue?
opts: Interleukins 4, 5 and 13, with eosinophil influx

Correct. This is type 2 inflammation, and naming the three interleukins is the molecular-mechanism objective in action. Polyps are benign, non-neoplastic oedematous masses from the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells.
Interleukin 17, with mast cell influx
Interleukin 17 and mast cell influx are not the polyp pathway. Polyps are type 2 inflammation driven by interleukins 4, 5 and 13 with eosinophils.
Interleukins 1, 6 and tumour necrosis factor, with neutrophil influx
That is the type 1 or acute inflammatory profile, not the type 2 allergic one.
Interferon gamma, with lymphocyte influx
A type 1 T-helper response, which is not what drives polyps.

A.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
A.q: What enlarges the inferior turbinates, and what does rhinitis medicamentosa refer to?
opts: Bacterial infection of the turbinate bone; osteomyelitis
Osteomyelitis of the turbinate bone is not among the triggers. Enlargement comes from venous engorgement, mucosal oedema or bony hypertrophy.
Cartilage displacement off the midline; a congenital deformity
That is deviated septum, an anatomical rather than mucosal problem.
Venous engorgement, oedema or bony hypertrophy; decongestant rebound

Correct. Three possible substrates, and the drug-induced one has its own name. It is the same rebound phenomenon that appears in ocular pharmacology — overuse of a vasoconstrictor leaving the tissue more congested than before.
Eosinophilic polyp formation; an allergic reaction
Polyps are a separate entity with their own type 2 mechanism.

A.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
A.q: How do petechiae, purpura and ecchymoses differ?
opts: By size — petechiae 1 to 2 millimetres or less, purpura 3 to 10 millimetres, ecchymoses greater than 10 millimetres — with similar underlying pathology
Correct. It is a single process of bleeding into the dermis described at three scales.
By mechanism — petechiae from capillary rupture, purpura from vessel dilatation, and ecchymoses from melanin deposition in the dermis rather than blood
The pathology is described as similar across all three.
By depth — petechiae epidermal, purpura dermal, ecchymoses subcutaneous
All involve blood in the dermis; the distinction given is size.
By blanchability — petechiae blanch, purpura and ecchymoses do not
All three are non-blanchable.

A.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
A.q: How often does the epidermis turn over, and what modifies that rate?
opts: Every 6 to 12 months, and considerably more rapid in older patients
Both the interval and the direction of the age effect are wrong.
Turnover ceases after adolescence
The epidermis renews throughout life.
Every 30 to 60 days, and turnover is more rapid in younger patients
Correct. Age-dependent turnover matters because it sets how quickly the epidermis can repair itself.
Every 24 to 48 hours, with no age dependence
That is far faster than the stated rate.

A.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
A.q: Pseudomembranous inflammation consists of a superficial necrotic layer made up of which components?
opts: Granulation tissue, proliferating fibroblasts and newly formed capillary networks throughout
These are features of healing and of chronic inflammation rather than of this pattern.
Fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris, forming a membrane-like covering over the affected mucosa
Correct. That covering over the mucosa is what the term describes.
Pus alone, without a fibrin component
Pus without a membrane describes the suppurative pattern.
Mucus, plasma and erythrocytes
Mucus hypersecretion defines the catarrhal pattern; erythrocytes feature in haemorrhagic inflammation.

B.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
B.q: What proportion of severe blindness from macular degeneration does the wet form account for?
opts: About fifty per cent
Below the true figure.
About twenty-five per cent
Well below the true figure.
About ten per cent
That inverts the figure.
About ninety per cent
Correct — despite the dry form being commoner.

B.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
B.q: Over what timescale does acute inflammation occur, and when does it begin?
opts: Over minutes to hours only, beginning after a full 24 hours have elapsed since the injury
The stated range is wider than this, and onset is immediate rather than delayed.
Over seconds, minutes, hours or days, beginning within seconds of tissue injury
Correct. Acute inflammation begins immediately — within seconds — following injury of tissues.
Over days to months, beginning once macrophages arrive
That timescale belongs to chronic inflammation, which is characterised by macrophages and lymphocytes.
Over weeks, beginning after antibody production starts
Antibody-mediated reactions belong to chronic inflammation.

B.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
B.q: What protects the outer third of the ear canal?
opts: Ciliated epithelium sweeping debris outward
Ciliated epithelium sweeps the respiratory tract; the ear canal clears itself by cerumen migration instead.
A keratin plug at the isthmus
There is no keratin plug at the isthmus. What sits in the outer third is cerumen and hair.
Cerumen from ceruminous glands, and hair follicles
Correct. Both sit in the outer third, which is why impaction and otitis externa are canal diseases.
Mucus from goblet cells
The ear canal is lined by skin, not respiratory mucosa, so it has no goblet cells to produce mucus.

B.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
B.q: Which cell types characterise chronic inflammation on review?
opts: Basophils and mast cells only
Basophils are responsible for allergic and antigen responses through histamine, and are not given as the characteristic chronic cell.
Fibroblasts in the absence of leukocytes
Connective tissue proliferation accompanies chronic inflammation but does not replace the leukocyte infiltrate.
Neutrophils and eosinophils predominantly, without mononuclear infiltrate
Neutrophils dominate the acute response; eosinophils are prominent in allergy and parasitic infection.
Macrophages, monocytes and mononuclear cells including lymphocytes and plasma cells
Correct. The review slide lists exactly these, accompanied by proliferation of blood vessels and connective tissue.

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: How do eccrine and apocrine sweat glands differ in secretion and function?
opts: Eccrine secrete keratin and apocrine secrete melanin
Neither gland secretes either of those.

Eccrine open onto the skin surface and secrete water and electrolytes for cooling by evaporation; apocrine sit mainly in the axilla and anogenital areas and secrete protein and fatty lipids, functioning as scent glands
Correct. Body odour comes from bacterial degradation of apocrine sweat, not from the sweat itself.
Eccrine glands sit in the axilla and anogenital areas and secrete protein and fatty lipids; apocrine glands open onto the surface of the skin and secrete water and electrolytes for cooling the body
This reverses the two glands entirely.
Both secrete sebum, differing only in the body regions they occupy
Sebum is the product of the sebaceous glands, which are a third type.

B.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
B.q: Which virus causes conjunctivitis?
opts: Herpes simplex virus
That deck entry is for epithelial keratitis.
Varicella zoster virus
That appears under herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus does not cause conjunctivitis.
Adenovirus
Correct — adenovirus.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: What defines telangiectasia at the tissue level?
opts: Capillary rupture with blood deposited into the dermis
That produces petechiae and purpura.
Dense inflammatory infiltration around dilated vessels
There is specifically no inflammatory infiltration.
Proliferation of new vessels driven by release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the surrounding dermis over a prolonged period
That mechanism is described for nail clubbing.
Permanent dilatation and thinning of the endothelium of capillaries, venules and arterioles in the superficial dermis, with NO inflammatory cell infiltration
Correct. The absence of inflammatory infiltrate is the discriminating feature.

B.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
B.q: In the reviewed sequence of acute inflammation, which vascular event comes FIRST?
opts: Increased vascular permeability
Permeability rises third, after both vascular calibre changes.
Haemoconcentration and stasis
These follow the permeability change, as fluid leaves the vessel.
Vasoconstriction
Correct. The sequence opens with vasoconstriction, followed by vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, then haemoconcentration and stasis.
Vasodilation
Vasodilation is second, following the initial vasoconstriction.

B.io: l — Describe the tumor, nodes, metastases (TNM) staging system
B.q: What important caveat attaches to TNM definitions?
opts: They replace histological grading, which is no longer used
Staging and grading answer different questions and both remain.
They are cancer-specific; for some cancers depth of invasion matters more than size
Correct — which is why a staging table applies to one named cancer rather than all.
They are identical across every cancer, which is what makes the system universal
The definitions are cancer-specific, not identical across cancers.
They apply only to epithelial malignancies and not to sarcomas
No such restriction is stated.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
B.q: Which three interneuron types modulate the retinal signal before it reaches the ganglion cells?
opts: Horizontal, amacrine and Purkinje cells
Purkinje cells are cerebellar.
Rod, cone and ganglion cells
Those are the input and output, not the interneurons between them.
Bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells
Correct — those three make up the modulating network.
Bipolar, Müller and astrocyte cells
Müller cells and astrocytes are supporting glia, not the modulating trio.

B.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
B.q: Which cancer patients are described as sometimes carrying an inherited mutation of BRCA-1 or BRCA-2?
opts: The majority of breast cancer patients
It is a minority.
All patients with familial adenomatous polyposis
That syndrome follows from adenomatous polyposis coli.
All patients with xeroderma pigmentosum
That follows from a different set of repair genes.
A minority of breast cancer patients
Correct — a minority, not most.

B.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: What causes an organ to enlarge in hypertrophy, and where is it especially important?
opts: An increase in the number of cells; especially important in labile tissues such as epithelium and bone marrow
That describes hyperplasia rather than hypertrophy.
Replacement of one mature cell type by another; especially important at epithelial junctions
That describes metaplasia.
Autonomous proliferation of a clone of cells; especially important in glandular tissue
That describes a neoplasm.
Enlargement of the individual cells; especially important in permanent tissues such as skeletal and cardiac muscle
Correct — it may also occur in other tissues as part of adaptive growth.

B.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
B.q: What is a fissure, and what conditions produce one?
opts: A linear ulcer forming a crack in the epidermis, from loss of elasticity or flexibility, severe dryness and mechanical tension, with hyperkeratosis thickening the stratum corneum
Correct. It is a linear form of ulceration rather than a distinct process.
A superficial loss of the epidermis that spares the dermal-epidermal junction and everything beneath it, so no collagen is ever destroyed in the process of healing
That is an erosion, and it is not linear by definition.
A thickened plaque produced by chronic rubbing
That is lichenification.
A dilated superficial vessel without inflammatory infiltrate
That is telangiectasia.

B.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
B.q: What is the classic symptom tetrad of Meniere disease?
opts: Continuous vertigo lasting days, unilateral tinnitus, unilateral loss, and nystagmus
That is labyrinthitis — and the duration is the main separator.
Vertigo lasting under a minute on head movement, with no hearing loss
Otoconia loose in the semicircular canals is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief positional attacks and spares hearing.
High-frequency hearing loss with tinnitus and no vertigo
That is closer to presbycusis or noise trauma, neither of which is vestibular.
Episodic vertigo for hours, low-frequency tinnitus, low-tone loss, aural fullness
Correct. All four, and the LOW-frequency emphasis is what distinguishes the hearing loss from presbycusis or noise damage, which take the high frequencies first.

B.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
B.q: Which pairing of endogenous and exogenous toxic agents in chronic inflammation is correct?
opts: Endogenous — atherosclerosis; exogenous — particulates such as silica
Correct. Atherosclerosis is the endogenous example and particulates such as silica the exogenous one.
Endogenous — bacterial infection; exogenous — viral infection
Both bacteria and viruses fall under persistent infection, which is listed separately from toxic agents.
Endogenous — silica; exogenous — atherosclerosis
These are transposed: silica is an inhaled particulate and therefore exogenous.
Endogenous — rheumatoid arthritis; exogenous — lupus
Both are given as examples of autoimmunity, a separate cause from toxic agents.

B.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
B.q: What is the defect in conductive hearing loss, and where does it sit?
opts: Defective sound transmission, in the external or middle ear
Correct. The apparatus that carries sound inward has failed; the cochlea and nerve are intact. That anatomical split is what the tuning fork tests are detecting.
Central processing failure in the auditory cortex
Central pathways fall under the sensorineural heading in this comparison, not the conductive one.
Destruction of hair cells or auditory nerve fibres, in the inner ear
That is sensorineural loss — the sensing apparatus rather than the conducting apparatus.
Failure of glutamate release at cranial nerve VIII
A neural failure, so sensorineural by site even though the mechanism is synaptic.

B.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
B.q: Recognition and attachment during phagocytosis are enhanced by the presence of what?
opts: Serum factors known as opsonins
Correct. The review names opsonins explicitly, with immunoglobulin G and complement fragment C3b as the examples.
Histamine released from basophils
Histamine acts on the vasculature, causing dilation and increased permeability.
Fibrinogen deposited by the coagulation system
The coagulation system traps material in a fibrous network rather than enhancing recognition.
Bradykinin generated from plasma proteins
Bradykinin increases capillary permeability, causes pain, and may increase chemotaxis.

B.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: From how many cells is the proliferating population of a neoplasm derived?
opts: One cell, which underwent a genetic alteration
Correct — the whole population is clonal.
Many cells, each of which underwent an independent genetic alteration
The derivation is from a single cell, not many.
Two cells, one parenchymal and one stromal
Parenchyma and stroma are the components of the mass, not two origins.
A variable number, depending on the tissue in which it arises
It is one cell, without qualification.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 10

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: Which receptors carry the sensations of touch and pressure?
opts: Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles
Those are proprioceptive receptors of muscle and tendon, not of skin.
Langerhans cells and melanocytes
Langerhans cells are immune sentinels and melanocytes produce pigment; neither is a mechanoreceptor.
Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells
Correct. Meissner's serve fine discriminative touch and low-frequency vibration, Pacinian respond to deep pressure and vibration, and Merkel cells serve light touch.
Ruffini endings, Krause bulbs and free nerve endings only
Free nerve endings are named for touch, pain and temperature, but the three receptors listed for touch and pressure are different.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: Which signalling pathway does basal cell carcinoma overactivate, and in which cells?
opts: Uninhibited melanocyte growth at the dermal-epidermal junction
That is melanoma.
The Hedgehog signalling pathway, following ultraviolet-induced mutation of basal keratinocytes in the epidermis
Correct. It is the most common skin cancer and the most common malignancy in humans, slow growing and rarely metastasising.
The tp53 tumour suppressor pathway, acting in the differentiated keratinocytes of the epidermis
That is squamous cell carcinoma.
Fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, in immature keratinocytes
That is implicated in seborrhoeic keratosis, which is benign.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: Why are nasal polyps described as non-neoplastic?
opts: No new tissue is grown; existing mucosa becomes oedematous
Correct. They are waterlogged mucous membrane rather than a growth.
They arise from cartilage rather than epithelium
They arise from the mucous membranes of the sinus ostia or ethmoid air cells.
They regress without treatment in every case
Non-neoplastic describes what the tissue IS, not how it behaves over time or whether it regresses.
They are malignant but slow growing
Polyps are benign and not neoplastic at all, so describing them as slow-growing malignancy is wrong twice over.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: Why does psoriatic skin become dry?
opts: The stratum corneum is lost entirely
The granular layer is lost; the scale that remains is stratum corneum.
Sebaceous glands overproduce sebum, which dries the surface
Excess sebum relates to seborrhoeic dermatitis, and it does not dry the skin.
Epidermal cells fail to secrete lipids, producing xeroderma
Correct — the dryness follows from a secretory failure rather than from water loss alone.
Eccrine sweat glands are destroyed by inflammation
Sweat gland destruction is not described in psoriasis.

B.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
B.q: Roughly how many cones are there, and where are they concentrated?
opts: About 120 million, concentrated in the peripheral retina rather than the fovea
That is the rod population and its distribution.
About 6 million, spread evenly across the whole retina
Cones concentrate at the fovea rather than spreading evenly.
About 60 million, concentrated at the optic disc
The optic disc has no photoreceptors at all.
About 6 million, concentrated in the fovea centralis within the macula
Correct — that is the count and the location.

B.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
B.q: Which leukocyte is named in the exudate of acute inflammation on the review slide?
opts: The eosinophil
Eosinophils are tied to allergic and parasitic processes rather than to the general acute exudate.
The lymphocyte
Lymphocytes characterise chronic inflammation.
The neutrophil
Correct. The review describes exudation of fluid, plasma, proteins and leukocytes, with neutrophils named specifically.
The plasma cell
Plasma cells appear in the chronic inflammation review.

B.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
B.q: What kind of organism is Helicobacter pylori, and what does it cause in the stomach?
opts: A fungus that colonizes the gastric mucosa in immunosuppressed patients
No fungal cause is described.
A Gram-negative bacterium causing chronic gastritis
Correct — it colonizes the stomach and may lead to atrophic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia. It is the one bacterium among the microbial causes of cancer.
A Gram-positive bacterium that colonizes the stomach, causing acute ulceration and perforation
It is Gram-negative, and the process described is chronic rather than acute.
A virus that integrates its genome into gastric epithelial cells
The viral mechanisms belong to human papillomavirus, Epstein Barr and the hepatitis viruses.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 35

B.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
B.q: Which structures detect linear acceleration and gravitational position?
opts: The organ of Corti
The organ of Corti transduces sound into neural signals. It is the hearing apparatus and plays no part in equilibrium.
The three semicircular canals
The semicircular canals detect ROTATIONAL acceleration through cupula deflection. Linear and gravitational sensing belongs to the otoliths.
The otolith organs
Correct. They handle static and linear balance, while the semicircular canals handle rotation. The two systems together give the brain a complete picture of head position and movement.
The cupula and ampulla
Those are the sensing apparatus inside the semicircular canals, so again rotational.

B.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
B.q: Why does cerumen impaction cause conductive rather than sensorineural loss?
opts: It blocks the canal, so sound never reaches the conducting chain
Correct. The cochlea is untouched, and the defect is purely one of delivery.
It damages the outer hair cells
Wax sits in the canal and never reaches the cochlea, so the hair cells are untouched by it.
It stiffens the stapes footplate
Stiffening of the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a separate conductive mechanism entirely.
It loads the tympanic membrane with fluid
Wax sits in the canal in front of the membrane rather than behind it.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: Which property distinguishes the monocyte from the neutrophil in terms of sustained phagocytic capacity?
opts: The monocyte has a multilobed nucleus permitting repeated division
The multilobed nucleus is the neutrophil's feature, and is not linked to division here.
The monocyte can replace its lysosomal contents
Correct. The neutrophil cannot renew its lysosomes and dies after a few pathogens; the monocyte can replace its lysosomal contents and so keeps working.
The monocyte does not require opsonisation of its targets
Opsonins enhance recognition and attachment generally rather than being required by one cell and not the other.
The monocyte carries T cell receptors for direct antigen binding
T cell receptors are carried by T lymphocytes.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: A patient's inflamed tissue shows a leukocyte infiltrate dominated by cells with bi-lobed nuclei and pink-orange granules. Which process does this pattern most suggest?
opts: A chronic autoimmune process
Chronic inflammation is characterised by macrophages, monocytes and mononuclear cells including lymphocytes and plasma cells.
A humoral antibody response
Antibody production is mediated by B lymphocytes and plasma cells, which are agranulocytes.
An acute bacterial infection
Bacterial infection recruits neutrophils, which have multilobed nuclei and fine pale lilac granules.
An allergic or parasitic process
Correct. Bi-lobed nuclei with pink-orange granules identify eosinophils, which predominate in allergic reactions and parasitic infections.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: What is the mechanism of Meniere disease?
opts: Defective endolymph resorption causing hydrops, ballooning the scala media until micro-ruptures occur
Correct. Endolymphatic hydrops is the lesion: fluid accumulates because it is not resorbed, the membranous labyrinth distends, and micro-ruptures follow. The episodic nature follows from that cycle.
Inflammatory swelling and vascular congestion of the labyrinth after a viral infection
That is labyrinthitis, and the recent upper respiratory infection is what separates the two clinically.
Dislodged otoconia floating in the semicircular canals
Otoconia loose in the semicircular canals is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which produces brief positional attacks and spares hearing.
Demyelination of the vestibular nerve
Demyelination of the vestibular nerve is not one of the named mechanisms. The central causes given are brainstem stroke, multiple sclerosis and cerebellar tumour.

B.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
B.q: Why does a central chiasmal lesion spare nasal vision in both eyes?
opts: The macula is spared by a dual blood supply
Macular sparing belongs to occipital lesions.
The lesion affects only one eye at a time
A chiasmal lesion affects both eyes.
Only the crossing nasal retinal fibres are interrupted, and those carry the temporal fields; the temporal retinal fibres travel ipsilaterally and are untouched
Correct — the anatomy of the decussation explains which half is lost.
The lesion damages the temporal retinal fibres instead, and those carry nasal vision
Those fibres do not cross and are not caught by a central lesion.

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: Where does each step of vitamin D activation take place, beginning in the skin?
opts: Cholecalciferol is produced in the liver, then hydroxylated in the skin and finally in the kidneys
This reverses the order; production begins in the skin.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the skin and hydroxylated entirely within the kidneys in a single step
Two organs are involved in activation, the liver first and then the kidney.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the skin under ultraviolet B light, then hydroxylated first in the liver and then in the kidneys to the active form calcitriol
Correct. The skin only starts the process; two further hydroxylation steps in separate organs are needed before the hormone is active.
Calcitriol is produced directly in the skin under ultraviolet B light and requires no further modification in either the liver or the kidneys at all
The skin produces cholecalciferol, which is inactive until hydroxylated twice elsewhere.

B.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
B.q: Which epidermal layer forms the semi-impermeable barrier, and what is it made of?
opts: The stratum basale, a single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes at the base
That is the germinative layer, not the barrier.
The stratum granulosum, 3 to 5 layers of diamond-shaped cells
Those cells contain keratohyalin but do not themselves form the barrier.
The papillary dermis, a thin superficial connective tissue layer
That is dermis rather than epidermis.
The stratum corneum, 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes cemented together
Correct. That packing is what makes callused skin, and losing it is what makes barrier-defect conditions possible.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: What causes petechiae, and what size defines them?
opts: Minor bleeding into the dermis from capillary rupture, infection, thrombocytopenia or vasculitis, 1 to 2 millimetres or less
Correct, and they are non-blanchable because the blood sits outside the vessel rather than within it.
Permanent dilatation of the superficial dermal vessels, measuring 1 to 2 millimetres across the surface of the skin
That is telangiectasia, which blanches and involves no extravasated blood.
Increased melanin production in the basal layer, up to 5 millimetres
That produces a hyperpigmented macule.
Mast cell histamine release with plasma leakage, up to 5 millimetres
That produces a wheal, which is transient and blanchable.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: Which statement about neutrophils is correct?
opts: They present antigen to T cells after phagocytosis
Antigen presentation after phagocytosis is described for monocytes.
They are the predominant inflammatory cell in allergic reactions and in parasitic infection
Eosinophils are the predominant inflammatory cells in allergic reactions.
They are first responders to microbial infection, and their activity and death in large numbers forms pus
Correct. Both properties are given, and the second explains the composition of the suppurative pattern.
They mature in the thymus and carry T cell receptors
That describes the T lymphocyte.

B.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
B.q: In which cavity does seeding most commonly occur?
opts: The subarachnoid space
Seeding occurs there, but the peritoneum is the commonest.
The peritoneal cavity
Correct — the pericardial and pleural cavities and the subarachnoid space are also named.
The pericardial cavity
It is one of the named cavities but not the commonest.
The pleural cavity
Also named, but not the commonest.

B.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: What is a metastasis?
opts: Local invasion of a cancer into the tissue immediately surrounding it
That is invasion; metastasis means reaching a distant site.
A benign nodule that develops in the tissue draining a cancer
Metastatic deposits are malignant, being part of the original cancer.
A portion of a cancer that has migrated from the primary site to other sites
Correct — the primary remains where it began; the metastasis is what has left.
A second, unrelated primary cancer arising in another organ
A metastasis is derived from the original cancer, not independent of it.

B.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
B.q: What is the mechanism of the commonest, senile form of cataract?
opts: Progressive insoluble aggregation and deposition of lens crystallin proteins
Correct — the molecular mechanism of the ageing cataract.
Osmotic swelling of the lens driven by sorbitol accumulating inside it
That is the diabetic mechanism, which is separate.
Rupture of the lens capsule after blunt trauma
That is the traumatic mechanism.
Chronic ultraviolet-driven oxidative damage alone
Ultraviolet exposure is listed under environmental causes, not as the senile mechanism.

B.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
B.q: Why does asymmetrical vestibular input produce a false sense of motion?
opts: The brain reads the mismatch between the two sides as movement
Correct. Balance is a comparison, so unequal input is indistinguishable from turning.
Cerebral perfusion falls on one side
Falling cerebral perfusion produces dizziness and presyncope, which is the category vertigo is separated from.
The otoliths dissolve
Otoconia become dislodged in one condition, but they do not dissolve.
The cochlea sends conflicting auditory signals
The cochlea handles hearing and contributes nothing to the sense of position or movement.

B.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
B.q: What is the mechanism and character of a chalazion?
opts: An acute, tender, focal abscess of a gland sitting at the eyelid margin
That is a hordeolum.
A cholesterol-filled plaque along the nasal eyelid
That is xanthelasma.
Redundant lid skin with prolapse of orbital fat
That is dermatochalasis.
A chronic, non-tender, sterile granulomatous lipogranuloma of a blocked meibomian gland
Correct — sterile and granulomatous is what separates it from an infection.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: Why does prolonged antibiotic use predispose to FUNGAL otitis externa?
opts: It thins the canal skin directly
Antibiotics do not thin the canal skin. What they remove is the bacterial competition.
It removes the bacterial competition that normally limits fungal growth
Correct. The same logic as thrush: clear the residents and the fungus has the canal to itself.
It raises the canal pH to favour fungi
The association is not explained by pH. It is the loss of competing bacteria that lets fungus grow.
It damages the tympanic membrane
Otitis externa is a canal disease and does not begin at the membrane.

B.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
B.q: What is the globe geometry in myopia, and where does the image focus?
opts: The globe is normal but the lens has lost elasticity
That describes presbyopia.
The axial globe is too long, so the focal point falls in front of the retina
Correct — an elongated globe overshoots, focusing short of the retina.
The axial globe is too short, so the focal point falls behind the retina
That describes hyperopia.
The globe is normal but the cornea is irregularly curved
That describes astigmatism.

B.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
B.q: Who is the only one who can diagnose cancer?
opts: The radiologist
Imaging can suggest a cancer, but the diagnosis is histological.
The surgeon who obtains the specimen
Obtaining tissue is not the same as diagnosing it.
The oncologist who stages the disease
Staging follows a diagnosis that has already been made.
The pathologist
Correct — he said it twice. Grading is a histological judgement made on tissue.

B.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
B.q: What does it mean, structurally, for lymph nodes to be MATTED?
opts: They have lost their individual capsules and move as one mass
Correct. Tissue no longer respecting its own boundaries is why matting raises concern.
They are tender and mobile
Tender and mobile describes a reactive node responding to local infection, which is the reassuring picture.
They are smaller than normal
Matting is about nodes moving together as one mass, and says nothing about whether they are large or small.
They fluctuate in size with infection
Nodes that swell and settle with infection are behaving reactively, which is the opposite of the concerning pattern.

B.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
B.q: Beyond phagocytosis, what is the monocyte's role in the immune response?
opts: Secreting histamine to open the capillary bed
Histamine is attributed to basophils among the leukocytes.
Producing the fibrous network that traps exudate
That is the coagulation system's contribution.
Presenting pieces of pathogens to T cells so the pathogen may be recognised again and killed
Correct. This antigen-presenting role is what links the monocyte to later, faster responses against the same organism.
Restoring the immune system to its normal function once the infection has resolved
That is the regulatory (suppressor) T cell's role.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: What is the bone remodelling sequence in otosclerosis?
opts: Demineralisation of the ossicles from chronic inflammation
Not the described mechanism, and otosclerosis is not primarily inflammatory.
Fibrous scarring of the round window membrane
The lesion is at the oval window and the stapes footplate, and it is bone rather than scar.
Osteoblastic overgrowth of dense cortical bone without resorption
The sequence begins with resorption; it is remodelling rather than simple overgrowth.
Osteoclastic resorption, then spongy osteoid replacement
Correct. Bone is removed and replaced by soft vascular osteoid around the otic capsule and stapes footplate. The remodelled bone then fixes the footplate.

B.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
B.q: How is the avascular cornea oxygenated?
opts: By the choroidal circulation behind it
The choroid lies at the back of the eye and nourishes the retina.
By direct contact with air and tears
Correct — air and tears oxygenate an avascular tissue.
By diffusion from the limbal blood vessels alone
The limbal vessels do not supply the oxygen.
By the aqueous humour circulating through the anterior chamber
Aqueous nourishes the cornea and lens, but oxygen comes from air and tears.

B.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
B.q: What is metaplasia, and what provokes it?
opts: Change of one cell type to another under chronic irritation or injury
Correct — it involves a change in differentiation. Bladder transitional epithelium becoming squamous is the standard example.
Disordered growth of epithelial cells with variation in size and shape and loss of architectural orientation
That is dysplasia, which is the next step along and is precancerous.
Enlargement of an organ because its individual cells enlarge under increased demand
That is hypertrophy.
Autonomous growth of an abnormal mass of tissue derived from a single genetically altered cell
That is a neoplasm.

B.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
B.q: What produces lichenification, and what changes occur in the tissue?
opts: Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with accumulation of fluid between the two layers, forming a large blister that lifts the surface away
That is a bulla.
Slowing of keratinocyte division with elastin degradation
That is atrophy, which thins rather than thickens the skin.
Long-term scratching or rubbing of a pruritic area in an itch-scratch cycle, producing hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis with solid, firm, thick plaques without scaling
Correct, and lichen simplex chronicus is the named condition.
Loss of melanocytes across a circumscribed area
That produces a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo.

B.io: h — Describe the steps of chemical carcinogenesis
B.q: What do initiators do in chemical carcinogenesis?
opts: They cause permanent damage to deoxyribonucleic acid
Correct — permanence is what distinguishes initiation from promotion.
They cause sustained or enhanced proliferation of already-damaged cells
That is promotion, the second step.
They repair damage already caused by another carcinogen
Initiators cause damage; they do not repair it.
They trigger apoptosis in cells with damaged genomes
Apoptosis is the protective mechanism initiators help defeat.
