B.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
B.q: Besides cervical cancer, which malignancies is high-risk human papillomavirus associated with?
opts: Retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma
Those are associated with the retinoblastoma protein under heredity.
Anal, vulvar, vaginal, penile and oropharyngeal cancer
Correct — all five are listed alongside cervical cancer, the oropharyngeal one being a squamous cell carcinoma.
Hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric adenocarcinoma
Those belong to the hepatitis viruses and Helicobacter pylori respectively.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and certain B cell lymphomas
Those belong to Epstein Barr virus.
B.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 37

B.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
B.q: What is iris bombé?
opts: Forward displacement of the iris against the cornea
Correct — forward bowing of the iris closes the angle.
Backward displacement of the iris against the lens
The displacement is forward.
Atrophy of the iris stroma after an acute attack
That is not what the term means.
Adhesion of the iris to the corneal endothelium
That describes a synechia rather than iris bombé.

B.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
B.q: What causes Beau's lines, and what are they associated with?
opts: Impaired keratin synthesis, associated with deficiency anaemia
That is koilonychia.
A halt of keratin production producing horizontal or transverse grooves, associated with illness, stress, injury to the nail and malnourishment
Correct — the groove marks the period during which the nail stopped being made.
Overgrowth of connective tissue within the nail bed, associated with chronic liver disease and with diabetes mellitus in particular
That is Terry's nails.
Increased capillary density, associated with lung disease
That is clubbing.

B.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
B.q: On the dysplasia spectrum, what separates severe dysplasia from invasive cancer?
opts: The presence of mitoses, which appear only once invasion has occurred
Mitoses appear well before invasion on this spectrum.
Involvement of the regional lymph nodes
Nodal involvement is a staging question, and comes after invasion.
The basement membrane
Correct — carcinoma in situ sits above it and invasive cancer has broken through. The diagram runs normal, mild, moderate, severe, carcinoma in situ, then invasive cancer.
The degree of nuclear enlargement, which is greater in invasive cancer
Nuclear change is part of the grading, but the diagram turns on the basement membrane.

B.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
B.q: What happens to the vitreous with age, and why does it matter for detachment?
opts: It solidifies, pressing the retina more firmly against the pigment epithelium
The change is towards liquefaction, not solidification.
It becomes vascularised, bleeding into the subretinal space
The vitreous stays avascular.
It thickens and opacifies, blocking light before it reaches the retina
That is not the age change the vitreous undergoes.
It liquefies, so fluid can track through any retinal break into the subretinal space
Correct — Webster's jelly-in-the-fridge analogy, and the reason liquefaction is upstream of detachment.

B.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
B.q: A lesion of the optic tract produces which defect?
opts: Bitemporal hemianopsia
That is the chiasmal defect.
Monocular blindness
That requires a lesion before the chiasm.
Central scotoma with preserved peripheral vision
That pattern is macular rather than pathway-related.
Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia
Correct — site C. Past the chiasm, each tract carries the same side of both eyes' fields.

B.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
B.q: How are dermatofibroma and lipoma characterised in the tissue?
opts: Both are malignant proliferations of keratinocytes
Both are described as benign, and neither arises from keratinocytes.
Dermatofibroma is keratin-filled and lipoma is fluid-filled
Keratin filling describes an epidermal inclusion cyst.
Dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis; lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes
Correct. Both sit under the general term tumor, which describes rapid cellular growth and may or may not be malignant.
Dermatofibroma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes; lipoma is a fibrous tissue overgrowth within the dermis
This reverses the two lesions.

B.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
B.q: Histamine is described as which mediator in the inflammatory response, with what effects?
opts: The final mediator released during the whole response, causing fibrosis and the formation of dense scar tissue at the site
Fibrosis is a healing outcome rather than a histamine effect, and histamine acts first rather than last.
The first mediator of the initial inflammatory response, causing dilation of arterioles and increased permeability of capillaries and venules
Correct. Both the primacy and the two vascular effects are given.
A chemotactic factor drawing neutrophils to the site
Chemotaxis to neutrophils and monocytes is attributed to complement components.
An opsonin that coats foreign material for recognition
The opsonins named are immunoglobulin G and complement fragment C3b.

B.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
B.q: Histamine and serotonin share which pair of effects?
opts: Chemotaxis and opsonisation
Chemotaxis is attributed to complement components and possibly bradykinin; opsonisation to immunoglobulin G and C3b.
Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
Correct. Both are credited with dilating vessels and raising permeability, which is why they are the earliest vascular mediators.
Pain and fibrin deposition
Pain belongs to bradykinin, and fibrin deposition to the coagulation system.
Antibody production and antigen presentation
These are cellular immune functions rather than mediator effects.

B.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
B.q: Which physical law explains why a small septal deviation causes disproportionate obstruction?
opts: Boyle's law
A pressure-volume relationship for gases, not a resistance law.
Poiseuille's law
Correct. Resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius, so a modest narrowing has an outsized effect on airflow. That is why a deviation that looks minor can produce persistent obstruction.
Fick's law of diffusion
That governs diffusion across a membrane, which is a transport problem rather than a flow-resistance one.
Laplace's law
That relates wall tension to radius and pressure, used for vessels and alveoli, not nasal airflow resistance.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: What happens during the inflammatory phase of wound healing, and over what period?
opts: Days 1 to 3: type I collagen is laid down in basket-weave orientation
Collagen replacement belongs to remodelling, much later.
Days 1 to 3: a fibrin haemostatic plug forms, neutrophils and macrophages remove dead tissue, and growth factors and cytokines are secreted to signal the next phase
Correct. The phase both cleans the wound and issues the signal that starts proliferation.
Days 4 to 21: granulation tissue forms, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells that rebuild the wound bed from below over three weeks
That is the proliferative phase.
Days 21 to one year: type III collagen is replaced by type I
That is the remodelling phase.

C.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
C.q: Which vascular source accounts for anterior epistaxis, and what proportion of cases is that?
opts: The anterior ethmoidal artery, about 10 per cent
The anterior ethmoidal artery is not one of the two named plexuses. Anterior bleeds come from Kiesselbach's and posterior from Woodruff's.
Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall, about 90 per cent
Woodruff's is the posterior source and accounts for the minority.
Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum, about 90 per cent

Correct. Nine in ten nosebleeds are anterior and come from this plexus, which is why direct compression works so often. The posterior 10 per cent come from Woodruff's plexus on the posterolateral wall.
The sphenopalatine artery, about 50 per cent
The sphenopalatine artery is not how this is divided. The two named vascular sources are Kiesselbach's plexus anteriorly and Woodruff's posteriorly.

C.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
C.q: What is the symptom set of acute angle-closure glaucoma?
opts: Severe eye pain, headache, halos around lights, cloudy cornea, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, and nausea and vomiting
Correct — the full acute picture.
Painless gradual bilateral blurring with glare at night
That is cataract.
Flashing lights, a sudden shower of floaters, and a curtain falling across the field
That is retinal detachment.
Gradual central distortion with a scotoma
That is macular degeneration.

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: Ulcerative inflammation is characterised by which change?
opts: Formation of a membrane-like covering over intact and otherwise viable mucosa
That is the pseudomembranous pattern, in which the necrotic layer forms a covering rather than exposing tissue beneath.
Damage to blood vessels occurring with other exudates
That is the haemorrhagic pattern.
Coagulative necrosis of an entire limb segment
Dry gangrene involves coagulative necrosis, a separate and more severe pattern.
Necrosis and sloughing of surface epithelium, exposing underlying connective tissue
Correct. That exposure of the underlying connective tissue is what defines the ulcerative pattern.

C.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
C.q: Where does the gene damage in carcinogenesis come from?
opts: It is always acquired during life and never inherited
Inheritance is explicitly one of the sources.
It arises only from errors during deoxyribonucleic acid replication
Replication error is not the only source.
Inherited, and/or acquired from chemicals, radiation or microbes
Correct — the named sources are chemical carcinogens, ultraviolet and ionizing radiation, and microbial organisms: viruses and one bacterium.
It is always inherited through the germline and never acquired during life
Several acquired sources sit alongside inheritance.

C.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
C.q: What is the tissue basis of a papule?
opts: Focal loss of the epidermis that does not penetrate below the dermal-epidermal junction beneath it
That is an erosion, and it is a secondary lesion.
Hyperplasia of the epidermis with hyperkeratosis, plus inflammation and dense collagen fibres in the dermis
Correct, and seborrhoeic keratosis is the example given. A papule is elevated, solid, and under 5 millimetres.
Fluid containing inflammatory cells collecting within or beneath the epidermis
That is a vesicle.
Separation of epidermis from dermis with fluid accumulation
That is a bulla.

C.io: Describe the cellular changes associated with acute inflammation
C.q: Digestion of foreign material by activated neutrophils and macrophages involves which four steps?
opts: Vasodilation, exudation, stasis, and repair
These are vascular events rather than the steps of cellular digestion.
Adhesion, transmigration, aggregation, and chemotaxis
These are the steps that bring the cell to the site, before digestion begins.
Recognition, attachment, engulfment, and degradation
Correct. Those four, and recognition and attachment are enhanced when opsonins are present.
Opsonisation, complement fixation, lysis, and clearance
Opsonisation enhances the process but is not one of the four named steps.

C.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
C.q: Which features mark vertigo as PERIPHERAL rather than central?
opts: Absence of nystagmus entirely
Vertigo frequently presents WITH nystagmus and ataxia; its absence does not localise.
Gradual onset, vertical nystagmus, non-suppressible, with neurological deficits
Gradual onset, vertical non-suppressible nystagmus and neurological deficits describe CENTRAL vertigo from the brainstem or cerebellum.
Gradual onset with hearing loss and tinnitus
Hearing loss can accompany peripheral causes, but gradual onset and the other features listed describe central disease.
Sudden onset, horizontal or rotational nystagmus, fatigable, suppressed by visual fixation
Correct. All four point at the inner ear or cranial nerve VIII. Suppression by visual fixation is the one most easily tested at the bedside.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: What effects does serotonin have?
opts: Pain generation and leukocyte chemotaxis
Pain and possible increased chemotaxis are attributed to bradykinin.
Opsonisation of biomaterials
Opsonisation is performed by immunoglobulin G and C3b.
Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
Correct. Serotonin is given the same pair of vascular effects as histamine, which is why the two are grouped together.
Formation of a fibrous network trapping microorganisms
That is the coagulation system's contribution.

C.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
C.q: A benign tumour arises from cartilage. Which category does it fall into?
opts: Epithelial, since cartilage lines a surface
Cartilage is supportive tissue rather than a lining epithelium.
Glandular, so it would be called an adenoma
There is no gland of origin.
Neither, since the classification covers only epithelial tumours
The classification explicitly has a mesenchymal category.
Mesenchymal, since cartilage is supportive tissue
Correct — connective tissue, adipose, cartilage, smooth and striated muscle, and bone are all listed.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 16

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: How do hypertrophic scars and keloids depart from normal healing?
opts: Type I collagen is replaced by weaker type III in basket-weave orientation
That reverses the normal remodelling swap and is not the keloid mechanism.

Fibroblast dysregulation prolongs the proliferative phase, collagen deposition and degradation become imbalanced during remodelling, and collagen bundles develop haphazardly and exceed the boundaries of the initial wound
Correct. Two phases go wrong, and exceeding the original wound margin is the defining outcome.
Keratinocyte division slows and elastin degrades, thinning the tissue
That is atrophy, the opposite direction of change.

The inflammatory phase never resolves, so granulation tissue never forms at all and the wound remains open indefinitely without ever progressing to the proliferative or remodelling phases that normally follow
The problem is a prolonged proliferative phase, not an absent one.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: What happens to collagen during the remodelling phase, and how does the result differ from normal dermis?
opts: Collagen production continues to increase indefinitely
Formation of granulation tissue ceases in this phase.
Type III collagen is replaced with stronger type I collagen oriented in small parallel bundles, whereas normal dermis has a basket-weave orientation
Correct. The scar is strong but architecturally different, which is why it never quite matches the surrounding skin.
Type I collagen is replaced with weaker type III collagen oriented in a basket-weave pattern throughout the scar tissue that results
This reverses both the collagen types and the resulting orientation.
Collagen is degraded entirely and replaced by elastin
Elastin is not the replacement fibre in scar remodelling.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: Which lid deformity goes with dacryoadenitis?
opts: An outward-turning lid margin
That is ectropion.
A drooping upper lid from levator weakness
That is ptosis.
An S-shaped lid deformity
Correct — the characteristic sign of lacrimal gland inflammation.
An inward-turning lid margin
That is entropion.

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
C.q: What makes the eye the only place in the body where live neural tissue can be seen directly?
opts: The cornea contains myelinated tracts that can be seen on slit lamp
The cornea's nerves are not what makes this possible.
The sclera is thin enough to transilluminate the whole globe
Transillumination is not the mechanism.
The optic nerve head is visible through the pupil without cutting any tissue
Correct — the eye is a nervous window for exactly this reason.
The retina can be biopsied more safely than any other neural tissue
The point is that no tissue has to be cut at all.

C.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
C.q: What are the steps of haematogenous spread, in order?
opts: Cells separate and degrade intercellular tissue with enzymes, invade the vessel, then travel
Correct — multiple tumour fragments travel to other organs, so one organ may end up with several metastatic nodules.
Tumour cells adhere more tightly to each other; the mass compresses a vessel; a single fragment travels to one other organ
Cells separate rather than adhere, and multiple fragments travel.
Tumour cells enter lymphatic vessels at the margin and follow the natural route of drainage
That is lymphatic spread.
Tumour invades through an organ surface into a body cavity and settles on the serosal membranes
That is seeding of body cavities and surfaces.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 14

C.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
C.q: What can a hyperopic patient see well?
opts: Objects far away
Correct — hyperopia is farsightedness, so distance vision is the preserved one.
Objects up close
Near vision is the impaired one in hyperopia.
Neither near nor far without correction
Distance vision is preserved.
Only objects directly in the central field
Hyperopia is refractive rather than a field defect.

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: What is the main pathologic finding in nail clubbing, and what mediates it?
opts: A halt of keratin production at the matrix
That is Beau's lines.
Incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
That is leukonychia.
Increased capillary density, with increased release of vascular endothelial growth factor
Correct, and it is associated with lung, cardiovascular, liver and inflammatory bowel disease.
Overgrowth of the connective tissue within the nail bed itself over a period of time
That is Terry's nails.

C.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
C.q: What does falling differentiation mean for the behaviour of a tumour?
opts: Aggressiveness is unrelated to differentiation and depends only on stage
Staging and grading are separate, but he explicitly linked grade to aggressiveness.
It becomes more aggressive only once the basement membrane has been breached
Invasion is a separate matter from the grade.
It becomes more aggressive
Correct — an anaplastic carcinoma is very aggressive compared with a well differentiated one. Grading is a scale of resemblance, and prognosis tracks it.
It becomes less aggressive, because poorly differentiated cells divide more slowly
He said the opposite, and poorly differentiated cells are not slower.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: How is episcleritis best characterised?
opts: A vision-threatening emergency with severe deep boring pain and scleral melting
That is scleritis.
An infection of the corneal stroma
That is keratitis.
A granulomatous blockage of a meibomian gland
That is a chalazion.
A self-limiting inflammatory blush, not vision-threatening and without severe pain
Correct — in deliberate contrast to scleritis.

C.io: e — Compare and contrast the different types of benign tumors according to origin
C.q: What can an adenoma sometimes do that reflects its origin?
opts: Produce finger-like projections from the epithelial surface
That describes a papilloma rather than an adenoma.
Secrete the hormone or hormones produced by its gland of origin
Correct — the tumour retains a function of the tissue it came from.
Invade through the basement membrane into surrounding tissue
Invasion is a malignant behaviour, and an adenoma is benign.
Seed the peritoneal cavity through an organ surface
Seeding requires malignant invasion through the organ surface.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 16

C.io: f — Compare and contrast the different types of malignant tumors according to origin
C.q: What is a malignant tumour of mesenchymal origin called?
opts: An adenoma
An adenoma is benign and epithelial.
A papilloma
A papilloma is benign and epithelial.
A sarcoma
Correct — mesenchymal means supportive tissue, and the malignant form is the sarcoma.
A carcinoma
Carcinoma is the malignant tumour of epithelial origin.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 18

C.io: j — Compare and contrast the theories of heredity and carcinogenesis
C.q: Which tumours are associated with an inherited alteration of the retinoblastoma protein?
opts: Retinoblastoma, a rare childhood tumour of the eye, and osteosarcoma
Correct — the same tumour suppressor, two very different tumours.
Neurofibromatosis types 1 and 2, with tumours of the central and peripheral nervous system
Those follow from NF-1 and NF-2.
Malignant melanoma
That follows from p16, also called INK4a.
Familial adenomatous polyposis and colon cancer
That follows from adenomatous polyposis coli.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 39

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: What is the pathophysiology of actinic keratosis, and what does it carry a higher risk of?
opts: Benign proliferation of immature keratinocytes, carrying a higher risk for basal cell carcinoma of the head and neck region in later life especially
Benign immature keratinocyte proliferation describes seborrhoeic keratosis.
Human papillomavirus infection of basal cells, carrying higher risk for melanoma
That is verrucae vulgaris, and it does not lead to melanoma.
Autoimmune T cell infiltration, carrying higher risk for lymphoma
No such mechanism is described here.
Damage from excessive cumulative ultraviolet exposure leading to intraepidermal proliferation of dysplastic keratinocytes, carrying higher risk for squamous cell carcinoma
Correct — it is described as the most common precancer, which is exactly why the dysplasia matters.

C.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
C.q: Why does stasis of blood flow matter mechanistically in acute inflammation?
opts: It terminates the inflammatory response
The sequence continues through adhesion, transmigration, chemotaxis, aggregation and phagocytosis.
It precedes leukocyte adhesion in the sequence, as slowed flow allows leukocytes to contact the endothelium
Correct. Haemoconcentration and stasis sit immediately before leukocyte adhesion in the reviewed sequence.
It marks the point at which acute inflammation gives way to chronic inflammation in the tissue
Chronicity is defined by duration and by the persistence of macrophages and lymphocytes, not by stasis.
It reverses the earlier increase in permeability
Nothing in the sequence describes permeability reversing at this point.

C.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
C.q: What is the pattern of onset in presbycusis?
opts: Gradual, symmetrical and bilateral
Correct, and it is sensorineural. Asymmetry would point away from ageing toward a focal lesion.
Sudden and unilateral
Sudden unilateral loss points to labyrinthitis or a vascular event rather than to age-related change.
Episodic and fluctuating
Loss that comes and goes suggests Meniere disease, where endolymph pressure rises and falls.
Gradual but strictly unilateral
One-sided gradual loss raises acoustic neuroma rather than presbycusis.

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: Why does an ulcer scar while an erosion generally does not?
opts: An ulcer involves a loss of melanocytes from the basal layer which cannot be reversed once it has occurred in the tissue at any point afterwards
Melanocyte loss produces hypopigmentation and is not the ulcer mechanism.
An ulcer destroys collagen in the dermis, so healing must lay down new collagen; an erosion spares the dermal-epidermal junction and the dermis beneath it
Correct. Scarring is a dermal repair process, so a lesion confined above the junction has nothing to scar.
An ulcer is infected and an erosion is sterile
Infection is not what defines either lesion.
An ulcer is larger, and size alone determines scarring
Depth rather than size is the operative difference.

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: What are the three causes of chronic inflammation?
opts: Trauma, thermal injury, and radiation exposure
These are acute physical insults rather than the listed causes of chronicity.
Persistent infection, prolonged exposure to potentially toxic agents, and autoimmunity
Correct. These are the three given, with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus offered as the autoimmune examples.
Vasodilation, increased permeability, and exudation
These are the vascular mechanisms of acute inflammation.
Opsonisation of foreign material, phagocytosis by neutrophils, and enzymatic degradation
These are steps in the cellular handling of foreign material rather than causes of chronic inflammation.

C.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
C.q: Which vascular change is directly responsible for allowing fluid and blood proteins to enter the interstitium?
opts: Vasoconstriction of the draining venules
Vasoconstriction is the transient opening event of the sequence and does not increase permeability.
Endothelial contraction increasing capillary permeability
Correct. Endothelial contraction is what allows the increased permeability through which exudation occurs.
Haemoconcentration occurring within the capillary bed
Haemoconcentration is a consequence of fluid loss rather than its cause.
Vasodilation of the supplying arterioles
Vasodilation increases blood flow into the region but does not itself open the vessel wall.

C.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
C.q: Besides invasion into adjacent structures, which abnormal interaction is a step in invasion?
opts: Abnormal apoptosis of neighbouring stromal cells
Stromal apoptosis is not the named step.
Abnormal lymphatic valve function
No such mechanism is described.
Abnormal cell-substratum interaction
Correct — the cell's relationship with its own supporting matrix changes.
Abnormal cell-cycle checkpoint control
Checkpoint failure is a gene-alteration problem rather than this step.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 24

C.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
C.q: What defines vertigo, and what distinguishes it from dizziness?
opts: A hallucination of motion, with NO syncope
Correct. Asymmetry between the two sides is the mechanism, and the absence of syncope is the separator. Dizziness or lightheadedness is a non-vestibular sensation of impending faint.
A sensation of impending faint from cerebral hypoperfusion
That is dizziness or presyncope, driven by hypoperfusion, orthostatic hypotension or metabolic imbalance.
Any unsteadiness on standing
Unsteadiness alone does not distinguish the two; the hallucination of motion does.
Loss of consciousness preceded by spinning
Vertigo explicitly involves NO syncope. Loss of consciousness points away from a vestibular cause and toward cerebral hypoperfusion.

C.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
C.q: What makes the middle ear vulnerable to the pressure changes behind otitis media?
opts: It is an air-filled space vented only by the Eustachian tube
Correct. A sealed air pocket with one vent is why closing the vent drops the pressure and draws in fluid.
It has no blood supply
The middle ear is perfused. Its vulnerability comes from being a sealed air space, not from any lack of blood supply.
It is lined by keratinised skin
The canal is skin-lined; the middle ear is mucosa, which is what absorbs the gas.
It is fluid-filled and cannot compress
The middle ear is air-filled; the INNER ear holds the fluid.

C.io: h — Describe the steps of chemical carcinogenesis
C.q: Which chemical carcinogens are classically emphasised in occupational bladder cancer?
opts: Aromatic amines
Correct — polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons come from tobacco combustion.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
Those are the tobacco combustion products, which also cause bladder cancer.
Alkylating agents
Not among the agents responsible.
Asbestos fibres
Not among the agents responsible.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 31

C.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
C.q: What tissue makes up a scale?
opts: Dried sebum, cellular debris, blood or necrotic skin
That is a crust.
Thickened epidermis induced by long-term scratching
That is lichenification.
Focal loss of epidermis and dermis with destruction of the collagen beneath
That is an ulcer.
A compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum, varying in size and thickness
Correct, and psoriasis is the example given — which follows from its epidermal hyperplasia and loss of the granular layer.

C.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
C.q: Above what cup-to-disc ratio is optic disc cupping progressive?
opts: Greater than 0.8
Above the threshold.
Greater than 1.0
A ratio above one is not anatomically possible.
Greater than 0.5
Correct — that is the threshold for an increased cup-to-disc ratio.
Greater than 0.2
Below the threshold.

C.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
C.q: What is the mechanism of wet, neovascular macular degeneration?
opts: Extracellular lipofuscin debris accumulating beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
That is the dry form's drusen.
Fibrovascular membranes on the retinal surface exert traction
That is tractional retinal detachment.
Ganglion cell axons undergo apoptosis from raised pressure
That is glaucoma.
Hypoxia and inflammation trigger choroidal neovascularisation, and new vessels breach beneath the pigment epithelium into the subretinal space
Correct — from trigger through to breach.

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: Which skin cancer is described as the most common malignancy in humans, and how does it behave?
opts: Actinic keratosis, which is by far the most common malignancy occurring in human beings
Actinic keratosis is a precancer rather than a malignancy.
Basal cell carcinoma, slow growing and rarely metastasising, typically on the head and neck
Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common.
Squamous cell carcinoma, rapidly metastasising
Squamous cell carcinoma is second most common.
Melanoma, slow growing and rarely metastasising
Melanoma progresses through radial to vertical growth and can metastasise.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: What single feature separates a pterygium from a pinguecula?
opts: The pterygium encroaches onto the cornea; the pinguecula does not
Correct — Webster put it as crossing the limbus, and called this section important.
The pterygium is yellow; the pinguecula is triangular
The colour and shape descriptions are the wrong way round and are not the separator.
The pterygium is painful; the pinguecula is painless
Pain is not the discriminator.
The pterygium is bilateral; the pinguecula is unilateral
Laterality is not the separator.

C.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
C.q: Why does a lesion of cranial nerve VIII produce the same audiometric pattern as cochlear damage?
opts: Both add mass to the tympanic membrane
Mass loading damps the middle ear structures, which produces conductive rather than sensorineural loss.
Both stiffen the ossicles
Neither the cochlea nor the nerve has any mechanical connection to the ossicles, so neither stiffens them.
Both obstruct the canal
Obstruction blocks the external canal, which is a conductive mechanism rather than a sensorineural one.
Both sit beyond the conducting chain, so both give sensorineural loss
Correct. The category is defined by where the defect sits, not by which of the two structures failed.

C.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
C.q: How does human papillomavirus produce a common wart?
opts: It triggers mast cell degranulation in the dermis
That is the urticaria mechanism.
It digests keratin using keratinases and proteases
That is how dermatophytes behave.
It invades epidermal basal cells through microabrasions, leading to proliferation of the epidermis
Correct, and clinical variants of warts are often associated with distinct viral subtypes.
It infects the melanocytes that lie along the dermal-epidermal junction within the epidermis
That is where melanoma arises, and it is not viral.

C.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
C.q: How does dry macular degeneration affect vision?
opts: Rapid central vision loss over days
That is the wet form.
Loss of peripheral vision first, with the central field spared until late
That pattern belongs to open-angle glaucoma.
Sudden painless monocular blindness
That suggests vascular occlusion or optic nerve pathology.
Slow gradual loss of central detail, with distortion and a scotoma
Correct — metamorphopsia and scotoma, developing slowly.

C.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
C.q: How do the causes of anterior and posterior epistaxis differ?
opts: Anterior from hypertension and anticoagulation; posterior from digital trauma
The two aetiologies are swapped. Digital trauma and dry air are anterior causes; hypertension and anticoagulation drive posterior bleeds.
Both are caused predominantly by anticoagulation
Anticoagulation belongs with the posterior group; anterior bleeds are usually local.
Anterior from coagulopathy; posterior from low humidity
Reversed again: coagulopathy belongs with posterior bleeding and low humidity with anterior mucosal drying.
Anterior from local trauma and dry air; posterior from hypertension and anticoagulation
Correct. Anterior bleeds are local and mechanical; posterior bleeds reflect a systemic vascular or clotting problem, which is also why they are more profuse and carry airway risk.

C.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
C.q: Which hair type is regulated by androgens, and which grows independently of them?
opts: Lanugo hair is androgen-regulated; terminal hair is not
Lanugo is newborn hair and is not the androgen-dependent type.
All three types are equally androgen-dependent
The three types differ specifically on androgen regulation.
Terminal hair is androgen-regulated; vellus hair grows independently of androgens
Correct. Lanugo is the third type, the fine hair of newborns.
Vellus hair is regulated by androgens; terminal hair grows independently of them
This reverses the two.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: What is the natural course of a subconjunctival haemorrhage?
opts: Benign, resolving over one to two weeks with bruise-like colour changes
Correct — benign, resolving over one to two weeks.
Progressive, threatening vision within days
It is benign, not progressive.
Permanent, leaving a fibrovascular scar
It resolves.
Recurrent by definition, so it requires long-term ophthalmology follow-up
It is not recurrent by definition.

C.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
C.q: Which way does the nystagmus of labyrinthitis beat?
opts: Vertical and non-suppressible
Vertical nystagmus is a central feature, and labyrinthitis is peripheral.
Absent, because hearing rather than balance is affected
Labyrinthitis impairs both, and nystagmus is a listed feature.
Horizontal-rotary, with the fast phase beating AWAY from the affected side
Correct. The damaged side is under-firing, so the slow drift is toward it and the corrective fast phase beats away. Severe postural instability, gait ataxia and nausea come with it.
Horizontal-rotary, with the fast phase beating TOWARD the affected side
The direction is reversed; the fast phase beats away from the lesion.

C.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
C.q: What is the characteristic frequency pattern of presbycusis, and why does it impair conversation?
opts: High frequencies go first, taking the speech consonants

Correct. Consonants such as /s/, /f/ and /t/ are high-frequency sounds and carry most of the discriminating information in speech, which is why voices become hard to make out in a noisy room while still being audible.
Low frequencies go first, taking the vowels
That is the Meniere pattern — fluctuating low-tone loss — and it is not age-related.
All frequencies fall equally
A flat loss is not what presbycusis produces, and it would not preferentially damage discrimination.
Only frequencies above the speech range are affected
If the speech range were spared there would be no discrimination problem.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: What proportion of circulating serum proteins do complement components represent, and what are their listed actions?
opts: 25%; responsible for the formation of a clot at the site of the injury or lesion
Clot formation is the coagulation system's role.
10%; chemotactic to neutrophils and monocytes, with the cascade able to damage bacteria
Correct. All three points are given together.
50%; primarily responsible for oncotic pressure
No such figure or role is given for complement here.
1%; acting solely as opsonins
C3b is an opsonin, but the complement components are credited with chemotaxis and bacterial damage as well.

C.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
C.q: What is canalithiasis?
opts: Dislodged otoconia floating free in the semicircular canals

Correct. The crystals normally sit in the utricle. Once loose in the endolymph they strike structures and generate a false sensation of motion. Why they dislodge is not the examinable part — that they can is.
Accumulation of endolymph in the membranous labyrinth
Endolymph accumulating in the membranous labyrinth is the hydrops of Meniere disease, which gives hours-long attacks with hearing loss.
Inflammatory debris within the cochlea after infection
Closer to labyrinthitis, and it would impair hearing, which this does not.
Calcification of the stapes footplate
Calcification fixing the stapes footplate is otosclerosis, a conductive lesion of the middle ear with no vestibular component.

C.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
C.q: Roughly how many rods are there, and what are they for?
opts: About 120 million, for dim light and peripheral vision
Correct — that is the count and the function for rods.
About 6 million, for dim light and peripheral vision
Six million is the figure for cones.
About 120 million, for colour vision and sharp acuity
Colour and acuity belong to cones.
About 20 million, for colour vision in bright light
Neither the count nor the function is right.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: How do phagocytic cells recognise immunoglobulin G bound to foreign material?
opts: Through histamine receptors on the endothelium
Histamine acts on the vasculature and is unrelated to opsonin recognition.
Through Fc receptors that recognise the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G
Correct. Macrophages and neutrophils carry Fc receptors that bind the Fc portion of the antibody.
Through the complement receptors that bind to the C3b fragment
Complement receptors recognise C3b, which is the other opsonin, not immunoglobulin G.
Through T cell receptors on the phagocyte surface
T cell receptors are carried by T lymphocytes, not phagocytes.

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: Which pattern of inflammation is defined by mucus hypersecretion accompanying inflammation of a mucous membrane?
opts: Catarrhal
Correct. Catarrhal inflammation is mucus hypersecretion accompanying inflammation of a mucous membrane.
Pseudomembranous
Pseudomembranous inflammation is a superficial necrotic layer of fibrin, inflammatory cells and debris forming a membrane-like covering.
Serous
Serous inflammation is largely low-protein plasma occurring early or with mild inflammation.
Haemorrhagic
Haemorrhagic inflammation involves damage to blood vessels and occurs alongside other exudates.

C.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
C.q: What distinguishes a vesicle from a bulla, mechanistically as well as by size?
opts: A vesicle is solid and a bulla is fluid-filled
Both are fluid-filled lesions.
A vesicle contains purulent material and a bulla contains serous fluid
Purulent content defines a pustule.

A vesicle is up to 5 millimetres with fluid containing inflammatory cells collecting within or directly beneath the epidermis; a bulla is greater than 5 millimetres and involves separation of epidermis from dermis
Correct. The bulla represents a deeper plane of cleavage, not merely a bigger blister.

A vesicle is greater than 5 millimetres and a bulla is up to 5 millimetres in diameter, and the two share an identical mechanism of fluid accumulation entirely within the epidermis rather than beneath it
The sizes are reversed and the mechanisms differ.

C.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
C.q: Which patient group is at particular risk in keratitis, and from which organism?
opts: Contact lens wearers, from Staphylococcus aureus
It is Pseudomonas in contact lens keratitis.
Elderly patients, from Streptococcus pneumoniae
Not the group or the organism.
Immunosuppressed patients, from Candida
Not the group at issue here.
Contact lens wearers, from Pseudomonas
Correct — contact lens wearers, from Pseudomonas.

C.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
C.q: Which combination of effects does bradykinin produce?
opts: Increased capillary permeability, pain, and possibly increased leukocyte chemotaxis
Correct. Bradykinin is the plasma-protein mediator that adds pain to the permeability effect.
Vasoconstriction, reduced capillary permeability, and analgesia at the site
Each of these is the opposite of what is described.
Antibody production and antigen presentation
These are lymphocyte and monocyte functions rather than mediator effects.
Coagulation and trapping of exudate
That is the coagulation system's role.

C.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
C.q: What is the classic example of dysplasia, and what usually causes it?
opts: Barrett's oesophagus, usually caused by chronic acid reflux
That was his metaplasia example.
Endometrial hyperplasia, usually caused by excess oestrogen
That was his hyperplasia example.
Skeletal muscle hypertrophy, usually caused by resistance training
That was his hypertrophy example.
Cervical dysplasia, usually caused by human papillomavirus
Correct — he added that it might become archival one day because of the vaccine.

C.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
C.q: Which description matches the serous pattern of inflammation?
opts: Mucus hypersecretion accompanying inflammation of a mucous membrane surface
That is the catarrhal pattern.
Largely plasma with low protein content, occurring early or with mild inflammation
Correct. Serous inflammation is largely plasma, low in protein, and occurs early or when inflammation is mild.
Large amounts of fibrinogen forming a thick meshwork
That is the fibrinous pattern, removable only by fibrolytic enzymes.
Remnants of white blood cells, protein and tissue debris
That describes suppurative or purulent inflammation — pus.

C.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
C.q: Where do the pressure waves that begin hearing actually travel first?
opts: The cochlear duct itself
The duct holds the endolymph that is displaced, but the wave begins in the scala vestibuli.
The scala vestibuli
Correct. Stapes movement at the oval window starts them there, and they displace endolymph in the cochlear duct.
The semicircular canals
The semicircular canals detect rotation and play no part in transmitting sound to the organ of Corti.
The scala tympani
The scala tympani carries the wave later in its course, after it has passed the cochlear duct.

C.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
C.q: Which two malignancies is Helicobacter pylori associated with?
opts: Hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma
Those relate to the hepatitis viruses rather than to Helicobacter.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Burkitt lymphoma
Those relate to Epstein Barr virus.
Cervical carcinoma and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma
Those relate to human papillomavirus.
Gastric adenocarcinoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma
Correct — usually abbreviated to MALT lymphoma.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 35

C.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
C.q: Why does the vertigo of Meniere disease come in attacks rather than continuously?
opts: Inflammation resolves and recurs
Inflammation across canals and cochlea is labyrinthitis, and its vertigo is continuous.
Pressure builds until micro-ruptures occur, then re-equilibrates
Correct. The cycle of build-up and release is what makes it episodic.
The virus replicates in waves
Meniere disease is a disorder of endolymph resorption, not an infection, so there is no organism replicating.
Otoconia settle between episodes
Otoconia settling between episodes explains benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which lasts seconds rather than hours.

C.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
C.q: The term agranulocyte is described as somewhat misleading. Why?
opts: Because they are actually a subtype of polymorphonuclear leukocyte
Polymorphonuclear leukocyte refers to all granulocytes, which is the opposite grouping.
Because these cells acquire granules only after activation
The granules are present but non-specific; they are not acquired on activation.
Because their granules are visible only in chronic inflammation
Visibility is attributed to the nature of the granules, not to the phase of inflammation.
Because these cells do contain non-specific azurophilic granules — lysosomes
Correct. The name implies an absence of granules, but non-specific azurophilic granules (lysosomes) are present.

C.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
C.q: What do tumour suppressor genes do, and what are some examples?
opts: They promote regulated cell growth; the examples are growth factors and their receptors
That is the protooncogene category.
They repair damaged deoxyribonucleic acid; the examples are BRCA-1 and BRCA-2
That is the repair-gene category.
They trigger apoptosis in damaged cells; no specific examples are named
Apoptosis genes are the fourth category and are described separately.
They inhibit cell growth; the examples are NF-1, NF-2, retinoblastoma and adenomatous polyposis coli
Correct — losing them removes a brake rather than adding an accelerator.
C.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 29

D.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
D.q: Why does lung cancer metastasize to the brain? What is the vascular explanation?
opts: Cells from the lung travel retrogradely up the inferior vena cava
The inferior vena cava carries blood towards the heart from below.
Cells from the lung follow lymphatic drainage into the subarachnoid space
That would be seeding rather than haematogenous spread.
Cells enter the left heart and leave by the carotids
Correct — the lung sits downstream of the pulmonary circulation, so its cells reach the systemic arterial side and the internal carotid takes them to the brain.
Cells from the lung enter the portal vein, which carries them to the brain
The portal vein carries gastrointestinal blood to the liver.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Why can a neutrophil kill only a limited number of pathogens before dying?
opts: It converts into a macrophage after a single encounter
It is the monocyte that leaves the bloodstream to become a tissue macrophage.
It cannot renew its lysosomes, so it dies after phagocytosing a few pathogens
Correct. The inability to renew lysosomes is precisely why the neutrophil is a short-lived, single-use phagocyte.
It lacks the enzymes needed to digest the bacterial cell wall it engulfs
The neutrophil is described as very active in phagocytizing bacteria, so the enzymes are present.
It must first be opsonised before it can engulf anything
Opsonins coat the target material, not the phagocyte.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
D.q: What is inflammation?
opts: The death of tissue through coagulative or liquefactive pathways
That describes necrosis, which appears here only as a feature of gangrenous inflammation.
The reaction of vascularized living tissue to injury
Correct. The definition given is specifically the reaction of vascularized living tissue to injury — vascularity is part of the definition, which is why avascular tissue cannot mount one.
The proliferation of fibroblasts following any cellular insult
Fibroblastic scar tissue is one possible outcome of the process, not the definition of it.
The activation of the adaptive immune system by a foreign antigen
Adaptive immunity may or may not be involved; the contrast is between purely physical damage and injury that activates an immune response.

D.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
D.q: What gives the spinous layer its alternative name of prickle cell layer?
opts: Dead flattened keratinocytes packed into scales
That describes the stratum corneum.
Keratinocytes connected by intercellular connections called desmosomes, which form a spiny appearance
Correct. This layer also contains the dendritic and Langerhans cells that act as immune sentinels.
Keratohyalin granules that give the cells a rough and irregular outline when viewed on microscopy
Those granules define the granular layer above it.
Melanin granules transferred from melanocytes
Pigment transfer does not produce the spiny appearance.

D.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
D.q: Macular degeneration is the leading cause of new-onset blindness in which group?
opts: Adults over seventy-five in the United States
Correct — that is the epidemiology.
Adults aged twenty to seventy-four in the United States
That is the group for diabetic retinopathy.
Children and adolescents
Not a group affected by this condition.
Adults of any age worldwide
The claim is specific to an age band and country.

D.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
D.q: What is the functional consequence of presbyopia?
opts: Loss of peripheral vision
Presbyopia does not affect the visual field.
Loss of colour discrimination
Colour vision is not affected.
Inability to focus on near objects, so reading glasses or bifocals are needed
Correct — and that is the everyday presentation.
Inability to focus on distant objects, so distance vision blurs first
Near focus is what is lost.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: Which gene mutation is named for squamous cell carcinoma, and which histological features are pathognomonic?
opts: Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance and radial growth
Those features are described for melanoma.
Mutation in the tp53 tumour suppressor gene, with keratin pearls and epithelial pearls as pathognomonic features
Correct. It derives from keratinocytes, and immunosuppression is a notable risk factor.
Overactivation of the Hedgehog pathway, with pearly papules and telangiectasias
Those describe basal cell carcinoma.
Activating mutation of fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, with a stuck-on waxy and scaly appearance on the skin
That is seborrhoeic keratosis, which is benign.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: Henoch-Schonlein purpura involves which systems, and which patients?
opts: The skin alone, with no systemic involvement whatsoever, at any age at all
The whole point of naming it is that it is systemic.
Skin, joints, kidneys and intestines, commonly in children aged 3 to 10 years
Correct — an immunoglobulin A vasculitis, which is why it is not confined to the skin.
Skin and lungs only, commonly in older adults
Neither the organs nor the age group match.
Skin and liver, commonly in neonates
Those organs and that age group are not described.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Basophils are chiefly responsible for which response, and through which mediator?
opts: Antibody production, through immunoglobulin G
Antibody production is the role of B lymphocytes and plasma cells.
Cell-mediated immunity, through T cell receptors
That describes T lymphocytes.
Allergic and antigen response, through histamine
Correct. Basophils drive allergic and antigen response via histamine, which causes inflammation.
Parasitic defence, through major basic protein
Parasitic infections are the eosinophil's domain, and that mediator belongs to it too.

D.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
D.q: Which history most separates labyrinthitis from Meniere disease?
opts: A recent upper respiratory infection

Correct. Labyrinthitis usually follows a viral infection, so a cold last week points hard at it; someone who has not had a cold in years is likelier to have Meniere disease. Both can be unilateral, so laterality does not separate them.
The presence of sensorineural hearing loss
Both cause it. The duration of vertigo and the preceding infection are what differ.
Unilateral rather than bilateral symptoms
Both are usually unilateral, so this is explicitly not a discriminator.
The presence of tinnitus
Both labyrinthitis and Meniere disease produce tinnitus, so its presence tells you nothing about which one you are looking at.

D.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
D.q: What happens to proliferation once a cell has committed to differentiation?
opts: It stops entirely, and the differentiated cells become immortal
Immortality belongs to the stem cell; differentiated cells have a limited life-span.
It stays at the same relatively low rate as the stem cell
Proliferation after commitment is dramatic, not unchanged.
It becomes autonomous and no longer requires physiologic stimuli
Autonomy is a property of neoplasia, not of normal differentiation.
It can be dramatic, but those cells have a limited life-span
Correct — the stem cell itself proliferates slowly; the committed progeny do the expansion, and then die.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 21

D.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
D.q: By what mechanism does diabetes mellitus cause cataract?
opts: Excess glucose glycates the lens capsule until it ruptures
It is osmotic swelling via sorbitol, not capsular rupture.
Hyperglycaemia causes crystallin proteins to aggregate directly
Aggregation is the senile mechanism; diabetes acts through sorbitol.
Retinal ischaemia releases vascular endothelial growth factor into the lens
That mechanism belongs to proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
Excess glucose is converted to sorbitol, causing osmotic swelling of the lens
Correct — the metabolic mechanism.

D.io: c — Describe neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
D.q: How differentiated are malignant tumours?
opts: Always anaplastic
Anaplasia is the extreme end, not the rule.
Always well differentiated
That describes benign tumours.
Various degrees of differentiation
Correct — malignancy does not mean uniformly poor differentiation. Benign tumours are usually well differentiated.
Always poorly differentiated
They span a range rather than a single grade.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 13

D.io: e — Compare and contrast the conditions of the eye that are age related
D.q: Webster tied presbyopia to a letter in an examination mnemonic. Which, and what does it stand for?
opts: The R in PERRLA, for reactive
The R stands for reactive to light, which is not the presbyopia link.
The P in PERRLA, for pupils
The P is simply pupils.
The E in PERRLA, for equal
The E is equal.
The A in PERRLA, for accommodation
Correct — pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation. He quizzed the room on it.

D.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
D.q: How are acute and chronic rhinosinusitis defined by duration, and what commonly accompanies the chronic form?
opts: Acute under 2 weeks; chronic beyond 6 weeks, often with septal deviation
Neither threshold matches, and septal deviation is a separate anatomical problem.
Acute under 4 weeks; chronic beyond 12 weeks despite therapy, often with nasal polyps
Correct. The two thresholds are the definition. Acute disease is usually viral — rhinovirus or influenza — with secondary bacterial infection by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae.
Acute under 12 weeks; chronic beyond 6 months, often with turbinate hypertrophy
The thresholds are wrong: acute rhinosinusitis is under 4 weeks and chronic is beyond 12 weeks despite therapy.
Acute under 4 weeks; chronic beyond 12 weeks, usually with no mucosal change
The durations are right but chronic disease often comes WITH polyps rather than without change.

D.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
D.q: Exudation refers to the movement of what, and to where?
opts: Fibrin into the vascular lumen to form a thrombus
The coagulation system creates a fibrous network at the site of injury, outside the vessel, to trap exudate and microorganisms.
Leukocytes from the interstitium back into the capillary lumen
Leukocyte movement is outward, and is covered by transmigration rather than exudation.
Erythrocytes into the alveolar space
No such process is described; haemorrhagic inflammation involves vessel damage rather than exudation as defined here.
Fluid and blood proteins into the interstitial spaces
Correct. Exudation follows the increased capillary permeability produced by endothelial contraction.

D.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
D.q: Which organisms most commonly cause bacterial otitis media?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis
Correct. The classic middle ear trio. Viral causes are respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, influenza and adenovirus.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus
Those are the otitis EXTERNA organisms, accounting for 80 to 90 per cent of that condition.
Aspergillus niger and Candida albicans
Those are the fungal otitis externa organisms, often after prolonged antibiotics or humid conditions.
Group A Streptococcus alone
That is the usual bacterial cause of tonsillitis, not of otitis media.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: How do cisplatin and carboplatin cause permanent bilateral sensorineural loss?
opts: They cross-link DNA in stria vascularis cells, compromising endolymph ion homeostasis
Correct. The stria vascularis maintains the ionic composition of endolymph, and without that gradient transduction fails. Damage there is permanent and bilateral.
They fix the stapes footplate in the oval window
That is otosclerosis, a conductive lesion with no drug involvement.
They generate reactive oxygen species that destroy outer hair cells at the cochlear base
Reactive oxygen species destroying outer hair cells from the cochlear base is the aminoglycoside mechanism, and it takes the high frequencies first.
They inhibit prestin in outer hair cells
That is salicylate, and the effect is tinnitus rather than permanent loss.

D.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
D.q: A patient has thick, leathery plaques on the neck and forearms with no scaling, after months of scratching. Which secondary lesion is this, mechanistically?
opts: Ulcer, arising from focal loss of both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it
There is no tissue loss described here; the tissue is thickened.
Atrophy, from slowed keratinocyte division
Atrophy thins the skin, and this description is of thickening.
Lichenification, from hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis driven by the itch-scratch cycle
Correct. The absence of scaling is what separates it from psoriasis, whose plaques do scale.
Scale, from desquamating stratum corneum
Scaling is specifically absent in the description given.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which cells are the agranulocytes (mononuclear leucocytes)?
opts: Basophils, mast cells and macrophages
Basophils are granulocytes, and mast cells are not among the listed groups.
Lymphocytes (B cells and T cells), monocytes and macrophages
Correct. These three are grouped as the agranulocytes or mononuclear leucocytes.
Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils
These are the three granulocytes.
Erythrocytes, platelets and circulating plasma cells
Erythrocytes and platelets are not leukocytes at all.

D.io: i — Describe the pathologic process of macular degeneration
D.q: What is known about the pathogenesis of macular degeneration overall?
opts: It is a consequence of raised intraocular pressure
That mechanism belongs to glaucoma.
It is unknown
Correct — the pathogenesis is unknown for both forms.
It is entirely genetic
It is not entirely genetic.
It is entirely driven by ultraviolet exposure
It has no single cause.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: Why does a deviated septum cause epistaxis and loss of smell?
opts: Compression of the ethmoid arteries and the olfactory nerve
Neither is a described mechanism; the problem is airflow, not compression.
Turbulent airflow dries the mucosa; air misses the cribriform plate
Correct. Two separate consequences of the same disturbed airflow: local drying with fragile vessel breakdown on one hand, and failure to deliver odorant to the superior nasal vault on the other.
Chronic infection eroding the septal vessels and olfactory epithelium
Secondary bacterial rhinosinusitis can follow ostial blockage, but the epistaxis and anosmia are explained by airflow.
Autoimmune destruction of the septal cartilage
Autoimmune destruction of septal cartilage is a different disease process; the consequences here all follow from disturbed airflow.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: What happens to the wider nasal cavity opposite a septal deviation?
opts: It atrophies from disuse
The opposite happens. The wide side carries MORE airflow, so its turbinate enlarges to condition the extra volume rather than wasting away.
It develops polyps from the increased flow
Polyps arise from type 2 inflammation, not from airflow volume.
Nothing changes; only the narrow side is affected
The compensatory change on the wide side is specifically described.
Compensatory inferior turbinate hypertrophy
Correct. The wide side does more of the work, so its turbinate enlarges to condition the extra airflow — which can then narrow the only good airway the patient had.

D.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
D.q: Middle ear effusion and cholesteatoma impair conduction by which mechanism?
opts: Mass loading
Correct. Both add fluid or tissue weight that damps movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles. The chain is intact and mobile in principle, but it is carrying extra mass.
Stiffness effect
Stiffness is fixation rather than added weight; otosclerosis is the example.
Discontinuity
Discontinuity means the chain is physically broken, which neither of these does.
Obstruction
Obstruction blocks the canal before the drum — wax, foreign bodies, exostoses.

D.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
D.q: What is the mechanism of a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo, against a hyperpigmented one?
opts: Loss of melanocytes, against increased melanin production in the basal layer of the epidermis
Correct. Ephelides, café au lait spots and Mongolian spots are the hyperpigmented examples given.
Increased melanin production within the epidermis, as against loss of melanocytes entirely
This reverses the two mechanisms.
Capillary rupture with blood deposition in the dermis
That is the mechanism of petechiae and purpura.
Dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels
That is telangiectasia.

D.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
D.q: Which human papillomavirus subtypes most commonly cause cervical cancer?
opts: Types 1 and 2
Not the subtypes responsible for cervical cancer.
Types 31 and 33
It is types 16 and 18.
Types 16 and 18
Correct — of many genetic subtypes, these two cause the majority.
Types 6 and 11
Those are the low-risk types not named here for cervical cancer.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 32

D.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
D.q: Haemorrhagic inflammation is described as arising from what, and occurring in what relationship to other exudates?
opts: Epithelial sloughing, and replacing other exudates
Epithelial sloughing defines the ulcerative pattern.
Damage to blood vessels, and occurring together with other exudates
Correct. Haemorrhagic inflammation is damage to blood vessels occurring with other exudates.
Mucus hypersecretion, and occurring in isolation
That describes the catarrhal pattern, and haemorrhagic inflammation is not described as isolated.
Fibrinogen deposition, and preceding every other exudate pattern
Fibrinogen deposition defines the fibrinous pattern.

D.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
D.q: Which structure separates the external ear from the middle ear, and what does it do?
opts: The oval window, which passes energy to the cochlea
The oval window is the boundary between MIDDLE and INNER ear, driven by the stapes.
The round window, which relieves pressure
It sits at the cochlear end and relieves pressure waves; it is not the external boundary.
The Eustachian tube, which equalises pressure
The tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx rather than separating compartments.
The tympanic membrane, which vibrates and passes energy to the ossicles
Correct. It is the boundary and the first moving part of the conducting chain, which is why perforating it causes conductive loss.

D.io: Describe the vascular changes associated with acute inflammation
D.q: Which vascular event immediately follows increased vascular permeability in the reviewed sequence?
opts: Haemoconcentration and stasis
Correct. As fluid and protein leave the vessel, the remaining blood concentrates and flow slows — which is what allows leukocytes to marginate and adhere next.
Chemotaxis
Chemotaxis comes later, after leukocyte adhesion and transmigration.
Phagocytosis
Phagocytosis is the final step of the reviewed sequence.
Vasoconstriction of the arterioles
Vasoconstriction is the first event in the whole sequence.

D.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
D.q: Why are genes promoting self destruction of cells with damaged deoxyribonucleic acid necessary?
opts: To limit the total number of cells an organ can contain
Cell number control is not the reason given.
To supply nutrients to neighbouring cells as they proliferate
No such metabolic role is described.
To slow the rate at which stem cells commit to differentiation
That is a question of stem cell kinetics rather than apoptosis.
To stop the damage becoming permanent in dividing cells
Correct — apoptosis prevents a mutation being carried on into the daughter cells.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 30

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: What are the growth phases of melanoma, in order?
opts: Sensitization then elicitation
Those are the phases of allergic contact dermatitis.
Radial growth within the epidermis, then vertical growth penetrating the dermis, then increasing tumour thickness, then metastatic invasion of lymphatics and blood vessels
Correct. The shift from radial to vertical is the point at which depth begins to matter.
Vertical growth down into the dermis first, then radial spread within the epidermis afterwards once the tumour has thickened sufficiently to invade
This reverses the first two phases.
Inflammatory, proliferative, then remodelling
Those are the phases of wound healing.

D.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
D.q: What is the primary component of the dermis, which cell produces it, and what does it provide?
opts: Melanin, produced by melanocytes, providing ultraviolet protection
Melanin is a pigment made in the epidermis.
Collagen, produced by fibroblasts, providing tensile strength
Correct, with elastic fibres of elastin and fibrillin providing elastic recoil and flexibility alongside it.
Keratin, produced by keratinocytes, providing an impermeable barrier
Keratin is an epidermal product.
Elastin, produced by mast cells, providing tensile strength
Elastin provides recoil rather than tensile strength, and mast cells do not produce it.

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the neurological anatomy of the eye
D.q: Which two structures make up the fibrous outer tunic of the eye?
opts: The sclera and the cornea
Correct — the protective white coat and the clear refracting window.
The choroid and the ciliary body
Those belong to the uvea, the vascular middle tunic.
The retina and the retinal pigment epithelium
Those form the neurosensory inner tunic.
The iris and the lens
The iris is uveal and the lens is not part of a tunic.

D.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
D.q: Cerumen impaction, foreign bodies and canal exostoses all cause conductive loss by which of the four core mechanisms?
opts: Obstruction
Correct. A physical blockage stops sound penetrating down the canal. It is the first of four mechanisms, and the only one that acts before the sound reaches the drum.
Mass loading
That is fluid or tissue weight damping movement of the drum or ossicles — middle ear effusion, cholesteatoma.
Stiffness effect
That is impaired mobility of the ossicles or drum, of which otosclerosis is the example.
Discontinuity
That is physical disruption of the ossicular chain, from temporal bone fracture or ossicular necrosis.

D.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
D.q: What is the classical corneal finding in herpes simplex epithelial keratitis?
opts: A geographic ulcer with a hypopyon
That is not the classical simplex description.
A ring infiltrate in a contact lens wearer
That pattern is associated with other organisms.
A wedge of fibrovascular tissue growing across and over the corneal limbus
That is a pterygium.
A dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs on fluorescein staining
Correct — terminal bulbs included.

D.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
D.q: A nodule is greater than 5 millimetres. What tissue does it arise from?
opts: Fluid accumulating between epidermis and dermis
That describes a bulla.
Dilated superficial dermal capillaries with no inflammatory infiltration at all
That is telangiectasia.
Dermal-based tissue with dense collagen bundles, extending into subcutaneous tissue
Correct. Epidermoid cysts are keratin-filled, dermatofibroma is fibrous tissue, and a rheumatoid nodule is fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by histiocytes.
Superficial epidermis only, with no dermal involvement
A nodule is defined by its dermal and subcutaneous depth.

D.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
D.q: Which findings does orbital cellulitis show that periorbital cellulitis lacks?
opts: Erythema and oedema of the lid alone, held forward by the orbital septum
That is the periorbital picture.
Crusting of the lid margin with altered tear film
That is blepharitis.
A yellowish nodule that does not cross the cornea
That is a pinguecula.
Proptosis, decreased extraocular movement and a risk of optic nerve compression
Correct — all consequences of a post-septal collection.

D.io: f — Describe the pathogenesis of glaucoma
D.q: What is the mechanism of primary open-angle glaucoma?
opts: The iridocorneal angle stays open but microscopic resistance in the trabecular meshwork impairs outflow, raising pressure gradually
Correct — the angle is open; the obstruction is microscopic and downstream.
The iridocorneal angle narrows anatomically and blocks aqueous outflow suddenly
That is angle-closure glaucoma.
Aqueous production by the ciliary body increases sharply
The mechanism is impaired outflow, not overproduction.
The canal of Schlemm is congenitally absent
The canal of Schlemm is present.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: What is the mechanism of urticaria?
opts: Capillary rupture with extravasation of blood
That produces petechiae and purpura.
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine, producing wheals
Correct, and it may be acute or chronic with a wide range of triggers.
T cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity 48 to 72 hours after exposure
That is allergic contact dermatitis.
Dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation from ultraviolet damage
That is actinic keratosis.

D.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
D.q: Where do melanocytes normally sit, and what drives their malignant transformation?
opts: At the dermal-epidermal junction, with ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damaging melanocyte DNA and leading to uninhibited growth
Correct, and the risk is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance.
Within the stratum corneum, transformed by keratinase digestion
That describes dermatophyte behaviour, not melanocyte biology.
In the reticular layer of the dermis, transformed by dysregulation of the fibroblasts that reside within it over a long period of time
Fibroblast dysregulation is the keloid mechanism.
In the basal layer, transformed by Hedgehog pathway activation
Hedgehog activation is the basal cell carcinoma mechanism.

D.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
D.q: What is the tissue distinction between an erosion and an ulcer?
opts: An erosion is focal loss of epidermis that does not penetrate below the dermal-epidermal junction; an ulcer is focal loss of epidermis AND dermis, with destruction of collagen and infiltration of inflammatory cells
Correct. The junction is the boundary that separates them, and crossing it is what brings collagen destruction into play.
An erosion involves both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it; an ulcer is limited to the epidermis alone and spares the dermal-epidermal junction entirely, so it never destroys collagen at all
This reverses the two.
An erosion is fluid-filled and an ulcer is solid
Neither is a fluid-filled lesion.
An erosion is a primary lesion and an ulcer is a secondary lesion
Both are secondary lesions.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: What is the mechanism of labyrinthitis, and why does it impair hearing AND balance together?
opts: Dislodged otoconia striking structures in the endolymph
That is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, which spares hearing entirely.
Fixation of the stapes footplate
Otosclerosis, a conductive lesion with no vestibular component.
Inflammation across both the semicircular canals and the cochlea
Correct. The inflammation does not respect the boundary between the vestibular apparatus and the organ of Corti, so both fail at once. That simultaneous involvement is what names it otitis interna.
Defective endolymph resorption ballooning the scala media
That is the hydrops of Meniere disease, and it does not begin with inflammation.

D.io: d — Compare and contrast the routes of tumor spread
D.q: What determines where a cancer metastasizes?
opts: Venous blood flow, tumour and endothelial receptors, and genetic fitness
Correct — metastatic spread is NOT random but determined by these three.
Chance alone, since circulating tumour cells lodge wherever the vessel first narrows
Metastatic spread is not random.
The size of the primary lesion and the duration of the disease
Those affect staging rather than the pattern of spread.
The histological grade of the tumour and its rate of mitosis
Grade and mitotic rate describe the tumour, not where it goes.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 27

D.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
D.q: Why does a tumour mass grow faster than normal tissue?
opts: A lower proliferative fraction together with a lower rate of cell loss
A lower proliferative fraction would slow growth rather than accelerate it.
An unchanged proliferative fraction with a shorter individual cell cycle
The proliferative fraction is exactly what changes.
A higher proliferative fraction together with a lower rate of cell loss
Correct — both halves matter; it is not only that cells divide faster.
A higher proliferative fraction together with a higher rate of cell loss
A higher loss rate would offset the gain; loss is in fact lower.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 22

D.io: k — Describe the histological grading of cancer
D.q: Which four histological features move a tumour from the benign end towards the malignant end?
opts: Encapsulation, uniform nuclei, absent mitoses, and normal differentiation
These are the benign features, at the opposite end of the same spectrum.
Invasion, lymphatic spread, haematogenous spread, and seeding
Those are behaviours and routes of spread rather than histological features.
Initiation, promotion, progression, and metastasis
Those are stages of carcinogenesis rather than grading features.
Pleomorphism, abnormal nuclei, mitoses, and abnormal differentiation
Correct — these lie on a spectrum rather than a switch.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 23

D.io: d — Compare and contrast the conditions caused by abnormal shapes of the eye
D.q: What causes astigmatism?
opts: An axial globe that is too short
That is hyperopia.
Loss of lens elasticity with age, so the lens can no longer change shape
That is presbyopia.
Irregular corneal or lens curvature creating non-spherical focal points
Correct — which is why a single focal point cannot form.
An axial globe that is too long
That is myopia.

D.io: Compare and contrast mediators of inflammation and their functions
D.q: Which two mediators are plasma proteins?
opts: Immunoglobulin G and C3b
These are grouped as opsonins.
Fibrinogen and fibrolytic enzymes
Fibrinogen appears under the fibrinous pattern rather than in the mediator list.
Bradykinin and complement components
Correct. Both are listed under the plasma proteins heading, alongside the coagulation system.
Histamine and serotonin
