These are listed separately as the vasoactive mediators, ahead of the plasma proteins.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which two of the listed subsets both act against virus-infected and tumour cells?
opts: B lymphocytes and plasma cells
These mediate antibody production rather than direct cell killing.
CD8+ cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells
Correct. Both target virus-infected and tumour cells.
Monocytes and macrophages
These are phagocytic and antigen-presenting rather than cytotoxic in this description.
T helper cells and regulatory suppressor T cells
T helper cells activate and regulate other lymphocytes; regulatory T cells restore normal function.

D.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
D.q: What are vocal cord nodules, and what causes them?
opts: Unilateral pedunculated fluid-filled growths on the middle third, from a single severe strain
That describes vocal cord POLYPS, and the unilateral-versus-bilateral split is the main distinction.
Bilateral wart-like exophytic lesions from viral infection
Wart-like exophytic lesions from viral infection describe papillomatosis, which is a separate entity from the benign phonotrauma lesions.
Unilateral firm masses with cord fixation, from malignancy
Fixation and a firm mass suggest carcinoma, not a benign lesion.
Bilateral symmetrical calluses at the anterior third junction, from chronic phonotrauma
Correct. Repeated slamming of the cords causes basement membrane hyalinisation — literally a callus. Bilateral and symmetrical, because both cords take the same repeated impact at the same point.

D.io: i — Describe microorganisms' role in carcinogenesis
D.q: Which forms of radiation cause cancer?
opts: Ultraviolet B, and ionizing radiation
Correct — ultraviolet B is the wavelength that damages deoxyribonucleic acid directly.
Ultraviolet A only, together with infrared radiation
The ultraviolet form named is B, and infrared is not listed.
Microwave and radiofrequency radiation
Neither is named as a carcinogen here.
Ionizing radiation only, with no ultraviolet contribution
Ultraviolet B is named alongside ionizing radiation.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 38

D.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
D.q: Is the vertigo of labyrinthitis episodic or continuous, and how long does it run?
opts: Episodic, with attacks lasting several hours
That is Meniere disease. The hours-long discrete attack is its signature, and mixing the two up is the error this question exists to catch.
Episodic, with attacks lasting under a minute
That is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, provoked by head position.
Continuous, permanent and non-improving
It does improve, because the body resolves the inflammation; recovery just takes weeks.
Continuous, over days, improving across weeks

Correct. Someone comes in saying the room has been spinning for three days, not that it comes and goes. Continuous vertigo that slowly settles over weeks is the labyrinthitis pattern, because the body is resolving an inflammatory process.
D.cite: 5. ENT Clinical Pathophysiology_STUDENT VERSION.pptx, Slide 17 (slide says episodic; corrected in lecture)

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which leukocyte is described as the first responder to microbial infection?
opts: The eosinophil
Eosinophils primarily address parasitic infection and allergic reactions.
The B lymphocyte
B lymphocytes act through antibody production in the humoral response.
The neutrophil
Correct. The neutrophil is named as the first responder to microbial infection, defending against bacterial and fungal infection.
The macrophage
Macrophages derive from monocytes that have left the bloodstream, and dominate chronic rather than earliest inflammation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Which three cell types are granulocytes?
opts: Lymphocytes, monocytes and macrophages
These are the agranulocytes, or mononuclear leucocytes.
Neutrophils, basophils and eosinophils
Correct. These are the three granulocytes; polymorphonuclear leukocyte refers to all granulocytes.
Neutrophils, monocytes and B lymphocytes
Monocytes and B lymphocytes are agranulocytes.
Basophils, eosinophils and natural killer cells
Natural killer cells are described among the T lymphocyte subsets rather than as granulocytes.

D.io: c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
D.q: What forms during the proliferative phase, and what is it made of?
opts: A fibrin haemostatic plug, over days 1 to 3
That is the inflammatory phase.
Type I collagen laid down in parallel bundles, over days 21 to one year of remodelling
That is remodelling.
Keratohyalin granules within the granular layer
That is normal epidermal maturation, not wound healing.
Granulation tissue, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells, over days 4 to 21
Correct. Those three cell types supply clearance, matrix and new vessels respectively.

D.io: h — Compare and contrast the pathogenesis of retinal detachment
D.q: What are the symptoms of rhegmatogenous detachment?
opts: Gradual painless bilateral blurring with glare at night
That is cataract.
Severe pain with halos and a fixed mid-dilated pupil
That is acute angle-closure glaucoma.
Slow loss of central detail with progressive distortion of straight lines
That is macular degeneration.
Flashing lights, a shower of floaters, and a curtain falling across the field
Correct — photopsia, floaters, then the curtain.

D.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
D.q: Why does skeletal muscle hypertrophy rather than divide?
opts: Protein intake causes fluid retention within the muscle, so the organ appears larger
Fluid was not the mechanism he described.
Resistance training converts slow fibres to fast fibres, changing the tissue type
A change of cell type would be metaplasia.
Striated muscle cells do not divide, so each fibre gets larger instead
Correct — protein and resistance build more actin and myosin within the existing cells. Bigger fibres, not more fibres, which is the whole distinction from hyperplasia.
Resistance training recruits satellite cells, so the number of muscle fibres increases
An increase in cell number would be hyperplasia; he was explicit that these cells do not divide.

D.io: g — Compare and contrast the categories of gene alterations in carcinogenesis
D.q: What happens when a protooncogene mutates?
opts: It becomes a repair gene, which then introduces errors into the genome
Repair genes are a separate category, and mutation disables them.
It becomes silent, so the cell loses its ability to grow at all
The result is uncontrolled growth, not loss of growth.
It becomes an oncogene, which encodes oncoproteins that promote continued uncontrolled growth
Correct — the same machinery, with the brake removed.
It becomes a tumour suppressor gene, which then inhibits cell growth excessively
Tumour suppressor genes are a separate category, and they are lost rather than gained.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 29

D.io: a — Describe the molecular mechanisms of abnormal cell growth and differentiation
D.q: Which two abnormalities separate a tumour cell from a normal cell?
opts: Abnormal apoptosis, and abnormal deoxyribonucleic acid repair
Both are genuinely important in carcinogenesis, but they are not the pair on this slide.
Abnormal vascular supply, and abnormal stromal composition
Stroma and vessels are components of a neoplasm rather than this contrast.
Abnormal differentiation, and abnormal cell size
Differentiation is graded separately; cell size alone is not the contrast drawn.
Abnormal regulation of cell growth, and abnormal cell-cell interactions
Correct — the same slide also contrasts a normal stem cell with a cancer stem cell.
D.cite: Abnormal Cell Growth for posting.pptx, Slide 19

D.io: j — Describe visual field deficits according to the area of pathology
D.q: What causes an ipsilateral optic nerve lesion?
opts: Posterior cerebral artery occlusion in the occipital lobe
That is the occipital cause.
Temporal lobe surgery
That affects the optic radiation.
Trauma, optic neuritis and ischaemic optic neuropathy
Correct — the three causes at site A.
Pituitary adenoma compression
That is the chiasmal cause.

D.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
D.q: Where do T lymphocytes mature, and what surface structure do they carry?
opts: The thymus; T cell receptors
Correct — matures in the Thymus, hence T lymphocyte, and it carries the T cell receptor.
The bone marrow; Fc receptors
Fc receptors are described on phagocytic cells recognising immunoglobulin G.
The spleen; complement receptors
Complement receptors are described on immune cells recognising C3b.
The lymph nodes; major histocompatibility complexes
Neither the site nor that structure is given for T cell maturation here.

E.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
E.q: Above what sound level does long-term chronic exposure cause irreversible cochlear damage, and what is the cellular change?
opts: Above 120 decibels, causing tympanic membrane rupture
That is acute blast injury, a conductive problem, and a different threshold.
Above 60 decibels, causing endolymphatic hydrops
Endolymphatic hydrops is the lesion of Meniere disease, caused by defective resorption rather than by sound exposure at any level.
Above 85 decibels, by stereocilia degeneration and apoptosis
Correct. Both words matter: degeneration of the stereocilia and programmed death of the hair cells. Neither regenerates, which is why the loss is permanent.
Above 85 decibels, causing reversible stereocilia fatigue
The threshold is right but the change is not reversible — apoptosis is cell death.

E.io: g — Describe the pathogenesis of cataracts
E.q: Which medication class is a cataract risk?
opts: Chronic corticosteroids
Correct — chronic corticosteroid use.
Chronic beta-blockers
Beta-blockers do not cause cataract.
Chronic antihistamines
Antihistamines do not cause cataract.
Chronic statins
Statins do not cause cataract.

E.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
E.q: What are the two connective tissue layers of the dermis?
opts: Papillary, the thin superficial layer, and reticular, the dense deeper layer
Correct. The dermis is also where the blood vessels and mechanoreceptors sit.
Basale and spinosum
Those are epidermal layers.
Corneum and lucidum
Those are also epidermal layers.
The papillary and the subcutaneous, being the superficial and the deepest layers
The subcutaneous layer, or hypodermis, is the third layer of skin rather than part of the dermis.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: What produces leukonychia, and what else can cause it?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed
That is Terry's nails.
Increased capillary density with release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the nail bed tissue itself
That is clubbing.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed, usually harmless nail bed damage but also seen with heavy metal poisoning
Correct — white streaks or spots, also called Mee's lines.
A halt of keratin production, associated with illness and malnourishment
That is Beau's lines, which are transverse grooves.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: Which structural epidermal changes occur in psoriasis?
opts: Epidermal hyperplasia, loss of the stratum granulosum, and failure of epidermal cells to secrete lipids producing xeroderma
Correct. Losing the granular layer is what leaves the characteristic scale.
Thinning of the epidermis with slowed keratinocyte division
That is atrophy, the opposite direction of change.
Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with fluid accumulating between the two layers of the skin itself
That is a bulla.
Loss of melanocytes from the basal layer
That produces vitiligo.

E.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
E.q: Where must light be focused for an image to form?
opts: On the optic disc, where the nerve exits
The optic disc is the blind spot and has no photoreceptors.
On the lens itself, which then transmits the signal

On the retina, after refraction through the cornea and lens
Correct — that is how the image forms.
On the choroid, after refraction through the cornea alone

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: Why does anticoagulation favour POSTERIOR rather than anterior epistaxis?
opts: The posterior mucosa is thinner
Mucosal thickness is not what separates the two. The difference is local insult against systemic vascular and clotting factors.
The anterior septum has no blood supply
Kiesselbach's plexus supplies the anterior septum richly, which is exactly why anterior bleeds are the common ones.
Anticoagulants are concentrated posteriorly
Anticoagulants act on clotting throughout the circulation and are not concentrated in any part of the nose.
Posterior bleeding is driven by systemic vascular and clotting factors
Correct. Anterior causes are local insults to the mucosa; posterior causes act on the vessels and on clotting.

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: Depolarisation of the cochlear hair cell comes from an ion influx. Through what, and out of which fluid?
opts: Influx from the perilymph across the basilar membrane
The ionic gradient that matters is between endolymph and the hair cell, not across the basilar membrane.
Release from intracellular stores after glutamate binding
Glutamate is what the hair cell RELEASES onto cranial nerve VIII after it depolarises. It is the output of the cell, not a signal arriving at it.
Efflux into the perilymph through voltage-gated channels
Voltage-gated channels open AFTER depolarisation and drive transmitter release; they are not what depolarises the cell.
Influx from the endolymph through the tip-link channels
Correct. The endolymph is the reservoir, and opening the tip-link channels lets ions rush in. Depolarisation then opens voltage-gated channels and glutamate is released onto cranial nerve VIII.

Dry is coagulative necrosis; wet is liquefactive necrosis arising from infection

Surface receptors that bind the Fc portion of immunoglobulin G

Differently staining cytoplasmic granules that are membrane-bound enzymes acting in the digestion of phagocytized particles

E.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
E.q: A temporal bone fracture causes conductive loss by which mechanism?

Stiffness of the ossicular chain
Stiffness is the opposite problem — the chain is intact but cannot move.
Mass loading of the tympanic membrane
Mass loading requires added fluid or tissue weight damping the chain. A fracture removes continuity rather than adding weight.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: Which sequence correctly orders the three linked vascular mechanisms?
opts: Exudation, then vasodilation, then endothelial contraction
This reverses the causal chain entirely.
Vasodilation of arterioles, then endothelial contraction increasing capillary permeability, then exudation
Correct. Vasodilation raises blood flow, endothelial contraction opens the capillaries, and fluid and blood proteins then move into the interstitial spaces.
Endothelial contraction, then vasodilation of the arterioles, then leukocyte transmigration into the tissue
Transmigration belongs to the leukocyte sequence, and the order of the first two is inverted.
Endothelial contraction, then exudation, then vasodilation of arterioles
Exudation is the consequence of increased permeability, so it cannot precede the vasodilation that begins the sequence.

Producing antibody directed against antigens the host has encountered previously
Antibody production belongs to B lymphocytes and plasma cells.
Presenting phagocytosed material to naive T cells
That is described for monocytes.
Killing tumour cells directly through granule release

E.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies
E.q: Which systemic diseases are strongly linked to scleritis?

Rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and systemic vasculitis
Correct — those three.

E.io: b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
E.q: Which causes are given for bullae?

That relates to sebum production rather than blister formation.
Mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemical exposure and autoimmune reactions
Correct, with bullous impetigo as the bacterial example and bullous pemphigoid as the autoimmune one.
Increased melanin production and cumulative ultraviolet light exposure alone
Those produce pigmented macules rather than bullae.
Capillary rupture and thrombocytopenia
Those produce petechiae and purpura.

E.io: Objective 1 — Review the anatomy of the ear, nose, neck and throat system.
E.q: What do the semicircular canals detect, and how?
opts: Linear acceleration and gravitational position, via the otoliths
That is the utricle and saccule — the otolith organs — which handle static and linear balance.
Rotational acceleration, by endolymph bending the cupula
Correct. Three loops in the sagittal, coronal and transverse planes. The fluid lags behind the head, the gelatinous cupula bends, and the hair cell stereocilia inside it are stimulated.
Sound frequency, via the basilar membrane
That is the cochlea, a different part of the inner ear entirely.
Middle ear pressure, via the Eustachian tube
The Eustachian tube equalises middle ear pressure. That is a conduction function and has nothing to do with detecting head movement.

E.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
E.q: Which four cell types make up the epidermis, and which predominates?
opts: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells, with keratinocytes about 90 percent
Correct. Because keratinocytes dominate so heavily, most epidermal pathology is fundamentally a keratinocyte problem.
Fibroblasts, macrophages, adipocytes and mast cells, with fibroblasts predominating
Those are dermal cells; the dermis is where fibroblasts and mast cells live.
Melanocytes, Merkel cells, fibroblasts and histiocytes, with melanocytes predominating
Fibroblasts and histiocytes are dermal, and melanocytes are a minority population.
Keratinocytes and melanocytes only, in roughly equal proportion
Four cell types are named, and the proportions are far from equal.

E.q: What are the purposes of cancer staging?
opts: To measure how closely the tumour resembles the normal tissue it came from
That is grading rather than staging.
To identify which gene alterations caused the tumour
Staging describes extent, not causation.
To determine whether the tumour is benign or malignant
That question is answered before staging begins.
Extent of spread, prognosis, and guiding management
Correct — all three. Staging answers a different question from histological grading.

A tissue macrophage that removes dead cell debris and attacks microorganisms
Correct. Monocytes eventually leave the bloodstream to become tissue macrophages with exactly these roles.
A plasma cell that secretes antibody directly into the interstitium
Plasma cells arise from the B lymphocyte lineage in this description.
A fibroblast that lays down scar tissue
Fibroblastic scar tissue is a healing outcome, not a monocyte fate.

Correct — those five.
Diabetes, prior vitrectomy and retinal trauma surgery

Sarcoidosis, malignant hypertension and melanoma

Carcinomi

That is the aqueous component.
It anchors the tear film to the corneal epithelium
That is the mucin layer's role.
It carries immunoglobulin to the ocular surface

It prevents evaporation
Correct — which is why its loss causes dry eye.

E.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
E.q: Which causes are listed as CENTRAL vertigo?
opts: Presbycusis and noise trauma
Both are sensorineural hearing loss without a vestibular component.
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, Meniere disease and labyrinthitis
Those are the peripheral causes, along with vestibular neuritis.
Brainstem stroke, multiple sclerosis and cerebellar tumour
Correct. All involve the brainstem or cerebellum, which is why the nystagmus can be vertical and is not suppressed by fixation, and why other neurological signs appear.
Otosclerosis and cerumen impaction

E.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.
E.q: Which organisms cause 80 to 90 per cent of otitis externa, and what predisposes to the fungal form?
opts: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; fungal disease follows swimming
Those two are middle ear organisms, and swimming predisposes to bacterial rather than specifically fungal disease.
Moraxella catarrhalis alone; fungal disease follows trauma
Moraxella catarrhalis sits on the otitis MEDIA list alongside Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, not in the external canal.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus; fungal after antibiotics
Correct. The bacterial pair dominate, and Aspergillus niger or Candida albicans take over when the bacterial flora has been suppressed or the canal stays wet.
Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus; fungal disease follows steroid use
Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus are viral causes of otitis MEDIA; they are not what colonises an external canal.

As an X-linked trait

It is entirely environmental with no inherited component

As an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance

E.io: c — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common ocular pathologies

Pus in the anterior chamber

Blood in the anterior chamber

Fluid beneath the neurosensory retina

E.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
E.q: How do the neutrophil's nucleus and cytoplasm appear?

That is the monocyte.
Multilobed nucleus that may appear like multiple nuclei, with cytoplasm looking transparent because of fine pale lilac granules
Correct. Both the multilobed nucleus and the fine pale lilac granules are given.
Bi- or tri-lobed nucleus with a number of coarse granules
That is the basophil.
Bi-lobed nucleus with pink-orange granules

E.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
E.q: Which pair of conditions are examples of autoimmunity causing chronic inflammation?
opts: Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus
Correct. Both are named as autoimmune causes of chronic inflammation.
Atherosclerosis and silicosis
Atherosclerosis is the endogenous toxic-agent example and silica is the exogenous one.
Asthma and hay fever
These are allergic conditions used to illustrate eosinophil predominance.
Trauma and bee sting
These illustrate purely physical damage versus damage involving an immune response, in acute inflammation.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: What produces Terry's nails, and what conditions is it associated with?

That is clubbing.
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anaemia
That is koilonychia.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
That is leukonychia.
Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed, associated with aging, liver disease, congestive heart failure or diabetes
Correct — the nail is opaque except for a dark band at the tip.

E.io: Objective 5 — Compare and contrast the pathophysiological processes of hearing deficits.
E.q: In conductive hearing loss, which way does Weber lateralise and what does Rinne show?
opts: Weber to the affected ear; Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone
The Weber is right but Rinne is not — a normal air-over-bone ratio means the conducting apparatus is working.
Weber is equal; Rinne shows bone greater than air bilaterally
An equal Weber implies symmetry, which a unilateral conductive loss does not have.
Weber to the AFFECTED ear; Rinne shows bone conduction greater than air
Correct. The blocked ear is not receiving competing air-borne sound, so bone-conducted sound is heard more loudly in it — and with the conducting chain impaired, bone beats air on Rinne.
Weber to the UNAFFECTED ear; Rinne shows air conduction greater than bone
That is the sensorineural pattern: the damaged cochlea cannot hear either route well, so Weber goes to the better ear and Rinne keeps its normal ratio.

E.io: Describe the various types and etiologies of inflammation
E.q: Suppurative (purulent) inflammation contains which combination of material?
opts: Remnants of white blood cells, protein and tissue debris — that is, pus
Correct. That is the suppurative or purulent pattern.
Fibrinogen forming a thick meshwork over the serosal surface
That is the fibrinous pattern.
Low-protein plasma with minimal cellular content
That is the serous pattern.
A superficial necrotic layer forming a membrane over affected mucosa
That is the pseudomembranous pattern.

It is limited to the anterior segment and spares the vitreous

It spares the sclera

E.q: What is sebum primarily composed of?

Triglycerides, wax esters and squalene

Water, sodium and chloride electrolytes

Keratin and keratohyalin
Those are epidermal structural proteins.

Both have ragged borders, and they are distinguished only by whether they metastasize

Benign is well circumscribed and compresses; malignant is ragged and invades
Correct — the benign tumour pushes surrounding tissue aside, the malignant one infiltrates and goes through it.

Correct, and a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble the lesion it came from.
A primary lesion is palpable and a secondary lesion is flat
Palpability separates macules from papules within the primary group; it is not the primary-versus-secondary distinction.
A primary lesion is benign and a secondary lesion is malignant

The distinction is about modification, not location or sequence of appearance.

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: What kind of immune reaction is allergic rhinitis, and what does it look like?
opts: Immune complex deposition, type 3 hypersensitivity
Immune complex deposition is type 3 hypersensitivity. Allergic rhinitis is type 1, immediate and IgE-mediated on the nasal mucosa.
T cell mediated, type 4 delayed hypersensitivity

IgE-mediated type 1 hypersensitivity, with CLEAR rhinorrhoea

IgG-mediated type 2 hypersensitivity with purulent rhinorrhoea

E.io: Compare and contrast the mechanism of white blood cells in the inflammatory response
E.q: What colour do eosinophil granules characteristically assume, and what is the nuclear shape?
opts: No visible granules, kidney-shaped nucleus

Pale lilac granules, multilobed nucleus

Coarse dark granules, bi- or tri-lobed nucleus
That describes the basophil.
Pink-orange granules, bi-lobed nucleus
Correct. The cytoplasm is full of granules that assume a characteristic pink-orange colour, with a bi-lobed nucleus.

E.io: a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
E.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the site of cellular division?
opts: The stratum corneum, the outermost layer
The stratum corneum is 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes; nothing divides there.
The granular layer, known as the stratum granulosum
That layer contains keratohyalin granules and sits above the dividing layer.
The stratum lucidum
That is 2 to 3 layers of flattened dead keratinocytes.
The basal layer, or stratum basale, the deepest layer
Correct. A single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes, which also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: Vasodilation of the arterioles supplying an injured region produces which immediate effect?
opts: Increased blood flow to the injured region
Correct. Vasodilation of the supplying arterioles increases blood flow.
Reduced hydrostatic pressure within the capillary bed

Contraction of the capillary endothelium
Endothelial contraction is a separate mechanism that follows, allowing increased permeability.
Movement of blood proteins into the interstitium

E.io: b — Describe non-neoplastic abnormalities of cell growth
E.q: What is the classic clinical example of metaplasia, and what changes into what?
opts: Endometrial hyperplasia — glandular becomes squamous under excess oestrogen
He used endometrial hyperplasia to illustrate hyperplasia, not metaplasia.
Barrett's oesophagus — squamous becomes columnar under chronic acid reflux
Correct — the lower oesophagus is squamous and cannot resist acid, so chronic reflux drives the change.
Barrett's oesophagus — columnar becomes squamous under chronic acid reflux

Cervical dysplasia — squamous becomes columnar under human papillomavirus infection

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: In the five main processes of the inflammatory response, what immediately follows the migration of neutrophils?
opts: Chemotaxis
Correct. The order runs increased blood flow, increased permeability, migration of neutrophils, chemotaxis, then leucocyte recruitment and activation.
Increased permeability
Increased permeability is the second process and precedes neutrophil migration.
Exudation of plasma proteins
Exudation is described under the vascular mechanisms rather than as one of the five numbered processes.
Increased blood flow
Increased blood flow is the first process, well before neutrophil migration.

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
E.q: Which factors contribute to seborrhoeic dermatitis, and where does it occur?
opts: Autoimmune T cell activation, affecting the elbows and knees

Ultraviolet damage, affecting sun-exposed skin
That is actinic keratosis.
Cutaneous microbiome dysbiosis, altered immune response and epidermal barrier dysfunction, affecting regions rich in sebaceous glands — scalp, face and upper trunk

A single fungal pathogen acting alone, affecting mainly the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet rather than the sebaceous areas of the skin

E.io: d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions

They release histamine from mast cells producing wheals

They proliferate within the dermis, digesting collagen

E.io: Objective 2 — Review the ear, nose, neck, and throat pathology.

Cannot be assessed; none; increasing number and range involved

E.io: b — Describe the physiological processes of vision
E.q: What does aqueous humour nourish?

The avascular lens and cornea
Correct — the avascular lens and cornea.
The retina and the choroid

The optic nerve head

E.io: Objective 4 — Differentiate the pathogenesis of vertigo and dizziness.
E.q: Which feature of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo separates it most cleanly from the other peripheral causes?
opts: The vertigo lasts several hours

It follows a viral upper respiratory infection
A preceding viral upper respiratory infection points at labyrinthitis, which also takes the hearing with it — unlike positional vertigo.
There is NO hearing loss

E.io: Describe the molecular mechanisms of inflammatory processes
E.q: Through which two routes can the inflammatory process heal an injury or implant site?
opts: Vasoconstriction of the supplying arterioles, or lymphatic drainage of the exudate
Vasoconstriction is a transient early vascular event and lymphatic drainage is not offered as a healing route here.
Generation of new tissue by native parenchymal cells, or formation of fibroblastic scar tissue
Correct. Those are the two outcomes of the sequence that heals the site.
Phagocytosis by neutrophils alone, or opsonisation by immunoglobulin G
Both are steps within the response rather than the tissue outcomes of healing.
Hemoconcentration followed by stasis, or leukocyte transmigration
Both appear in the sequence of acute inflammation, but neither is a mode of healing.

E.io: Objective 3 — Describe the molecular mechanisms of common disorders of ear, nose, neck, and throat.
E.q: Which single event in otosclerosis produces the hearing loss?
opts: Erosion of the incus by the remodelled bone
Discontinuity would be a different mechanism; otosclerosis works by fixation.
Hair cell loss at the cochlear base
That is noise or ototoxic damage, and it would give sensorineural loss.
Accumulation of endolymph in the scala media
Fluid accumulating in the scala media is endolymphatic hydrops in Meniere disease, a sensorineural and vestibular problem rather than a conductive one.
Ankylosis of the stapes footplate
Correct. Once the footplate is fixed it cannot transfer mechanical vibration into the cochlear fluid, and conduction fails progressively. Fixation is the whole lesion.
